Founded in 2018, Touchland is known for its fragrance-led hand sanitisers and personal care products. Its Australian debut includes 13 products across its Power Mist hand sanitiser, Power Essence body and hair fragrance mist, and accessory ranges. The Power Mist Hydrating Hand Sanitiser is available in eight fragrances, while the Power Essence Hydrating Body and Hair Fragrance Mist features five scents, and the launch also includes Sanitiser Mist Cases in three colour options.  “Australia has one of the most exciting beauty communities in the world, and we’re thrilled to finally launch with Sephora, a partner that shares our belief that the products you use every day should look and feel as good as they perform,” said Andrea Lisbona, CEO & founder of Touchland. insights.core: 核心论点是渠道即品牌跨市场扩张的关键杠杆：Touchland 以丝芙兰澳洲为落地支点，把品牌势能转化为区域可得性。其重要性在于，小众品牌的国际化越来越依赖强势零售商的背书与分销网络，而非自建渠道，这重塑了新品牌进入新市场的成本与速度结构。
insights.action: 值得长期监测的是：跨境新锐品牌在渠道背书下的消费者认知转化效率，以及零售商品牌组合扩张对本土品牌份额的挤压节奏。应持续追问渠道背书能否替代品牌自建认知、本土感官偏好差异是否被渠道策略掩盖。
insights.viewCMI: 从 CMI 看，这是渠道结构与品牌组合竞争的缩影：丝芙兰以引入海外新锐品牌强化差异化选品，Touchland 则借零售背书完成从线上认知到线下可得的转化。折射的结构性趋势是美妆零售正从品类货架转向品牌孵化平台，渠道本身成为消费者心智入口。长期需追问：新市场消费者的品牌认知能否由渠道直接迁移，跨境品牌的本土相关性是否被高估，以及货架扩容对本土新品牌的挤出效应。

insights.title: Federal sunscreen SPF-rating reforms raise cost concerns
insights.summary: 美国联邦层面拟改革防晒产品SPF标识与评级规则，报道聚焦合规与成本担忧。新规可能提高配方与测试门槛，抬高单位成本并压缩中低端产品利润空间，进而影响定价、货架结构与品牌竞争格局。规则不确定性下，企业需重新评估产品线组合与合规投入节奏。
insights.body: Search for: × Search for: Latest News Categories Baby Bakery Baking Beverages Breakfast Canned foods Cleaning & pest control Condiments Confectionery Convenience meals Dairy & eggs Deli Fresh produce Frozen Fuel Home & living Liquor Meat, poultry & seafood Pantry Personal care & beauty Pet care Pharmaceuticals Plant-based foods Snackfoods Stationery & games Tobacco Technology Automation Data & analytics Software & systems Channels Supermarkets Convenience Wholesale Direct to consumer E-commerce Hospitality Supply chain Distribution Warehousing Logistics Procurement Wholesale Manufacturing Operations Business Leadership Marketing HR Customer Finance Regulatory Sustainability Startups Login Subscribe Email Login + Choice, Accord Australasia and the Australian Sunscreen Association (ASA) welcome parts of the Therapeutic Goods Administration’s (TGA) proposed sunscreen reforms – but they are urging the TGA to assess the impact on costs and product access before finalising the rules. The organisation is calling for greater oversight of SPF claims after testing last year found 16 of 20 sunscreen products failed to meet their claimed SPF levels. Andy Kelly, Choice director of consumer impact, said the proposed reforms would require brands to test finished products, not base formulas, and submit results to the TGA before listing. insights.core: 核心论点是SPF评级改革把监管合规成本转化为行业结构性成本，而非一次性支出。成本压力将通过定价与SKU精简向上游与消费者传导，关键在于谁承担成本、谁借合规完成差异化，这决定防晒品类竞争格局的重塑方向。
insights.action: 值得长期监测的是：合规成本在价格带间的分布是否改变品类结构，以及消费者对SPF宣称的信任机制是否随监管收紧而迁移。应建立对功效宣称—价格—信任来源三者联动的持续观察框架，而非只看单次规则落地。
insights.viewCMI: 从CMI看，防晒是强监管、强功效宣称驱动的品类，评级规则变动会直接改写消费者的功效认知与比价逻辑。成本上升若转嫁为提价，可能加速消费分层：高端功效叙事与低价基础防护两端分化，中间价位带受挤压。长期值得追问的是，监管口径变化是否会让「SPF数字」这一外部信号失去部分说服力，品牌信任来源是否向成分透明度与第三方验证迁移。

insights.title: Coca-Cola lifts global margin and premium beverage share
insights.summary: 可口可乐在最新财报中同时提升全球利润率与高端饮料份额，显示其通过产品结构上移与价格/组合管理，在成熟品类中争取更高价值段。该信号对快消饮料行业具有风向标意义：增长重心从销量扩张转向价值捕获，高端化与利润纪律成为竞争主轴。
insights.core: 中心论点是可口可乐借高端饮料份额提升带动全球利润率上行，关键支撑是利润率与高端份额两项指标同步改善。其重要性在于验证了在碳酸饮料总量承压背景下，价值型增长路径可行，行业竞争逻辑或从份额争夺转向利润结构优化。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：高端份额的提升究竟来自真实感官价值差异，还是渠道与品牌溢价？应建立「高端化质量」的长期监测视角，区分结构性消费迁移与短期定价效应，避免把利润改善误读为需求升级。
insights.viewCMI: 从CMI视角看，这一信号折射的是饮料消费的「价值分层」而非单纯升级：消费者在总量上趋于谨慎，却愿意为特定场景、特定品牌支付溢价，高端份额因此成为利润杠杆。长期启发在于，快消增长越来越依赖对消费分层的精细识别与价格带卡位，而非覆盖式铺货；品牌需持续监测高端化的真实需求基础，警惕以提价替代价值创造的脆弱性。

insights.title: Yoplait Zero returns to shelves with a major refresh
insights.summary: Yoplait Zero 在经历配方或定位调整后重返货架，并以一次较大幅度的品牌与产品焕新重新面向市场。对无糖/低糖酸奶细分而言，这既反映主流品牌在健康化需求与口感期待之间的再平衡，也显示其试图以更清晰的货架识别与价值主张重建消费者关系；其成败将影响该品类健康线的竞争节奏与渠道信心。

insights.core: 核心论点是：无糖酸奶的竞争已从「有没有糖」转向「健康承诺能否与可接受的感官体验并存」。焕新本质是一次价值主张与产品体验的重新对齐；其重要性在于，主流品牌若无法同时满足健康诉求与口感底线，健康化细分就难以从概念走向稳定复购。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：健康标签的消费者信任是否正在从「零添加」转向「体验可信」？品牌应建立对减糖产品感官可接受度与复购行为的联动监测视角，并持续验证「健康承诺—感官体验—价格接受度」三者是否真正对齐。
insights.viewCMI: 从CMI看，这是一次典型的主流品牌在健康化细分中的「重新定位」而非简单上新：无糖/低糖已从差异化卖点变为品类入场券，品牌需以焕新重建货架识别与价格—价值叙事。折射的结构性趋势是健康诉求的「常态化」与消费者对「零」标签的审慎化，长期启发在于：健康线的增长不再靠标签红利，而取决于能否把健康主张转化为可被日常复购验证的稳定价值。
insights.viewSensory: 从感官研究看，「Zero」类产品的真正难点在感知机制：甜味缺失会放大酸感与发酵异味，质地稀薄与涩感也更易被察觉，因此焕新很可能涉及甜味体系、酸度平衡与质构设计的再校准。其范式含义是健康化不能只做配方减法，而需以描述性测评与偏爱性测试共同验证「减糖后的感官完整性」；长期启发是建立减糖产品的感官基准与持续监测，而非一次性调优。

insights.title: What should make a retailer pull a product from sale?
insights.summary: 文章讨论零售商在何种条件下应将产品下架，涉及食品安全、合规、质量投诉与声誉风险等触发因素。核心在于零售端作为产品流向消费者的最后关口，其下架决策既受法规约束，也受品牌与渠道博弈影响。对快消行业而言，这提示渠道权力与质量治理正成为零供关系中的结构性议题。

insights.core: 中心论点是：下架不应是危机后的被动反应，而应建立在可预警的决策标准之上。关键在零售端如何权衡合规、消费者安全与商业利益。其重要性在于，渠道掌握的产品准入与退出权，正成为产品质量治理与品牌声誉的实际守门机制。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：下架标准由谁定义、依据何种证据链？应建立渠道质量信号的持续监测视角，并重新验证「合规即安全」这一假设是否足以支撑消费者信任。
insights.viewCMI: 从CMI视角看，下架决策折射渠道权力向零售端集中的结构性趋势：零售商以消费者安全与信任为名，实际掌握了产品生死的裁量权，零供关系从交易博弈转向治理博弈。长期启发是，品牌需把渠道质量信号纳入市场监测，理解下架事件对品类信任与购买转化的溢出效应，而非仅视为单点危机。

insights.title: Woolworths’ continued value push drives sales growth
insights.summary: Woolworths 以持续的价值主张推动销售增长，反映在生活成本压力下，澳洲杂货消费者对价格与性价比的敏感度上升，折扣与自有品牌成为拉动客流与篮量的关键杠杆。此举亦加剧与 Coles、Aldi 等的价格竞争，重塑品类结构与渠道格局。

These sales followed a 0.5 per cent decrease in average prices, and a 6.6 per cent increase in comparable store sales. insights.core: 中心论点是：在消费趋紧环境中，持续而非一次性的价值投入能转化为销售增长。其重要性在于，它把「价值」从促销战术提升为长期定位，但摘要未给出增速、份额等数据，结论的证据强度有限。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：消费者对「价值」的定义是否已从价格转向「价格—品质比」？应建立对价格锚点、自有品牌渗透与复购质量的持续监测视角，而非以单次促销结果判断价值策略成败。
insights.viewCMI: 从 CMI 看，这折射出价值敏感从周期性防御转为结构性常态：消费者价格记忆被重塑，愿意为「够好且便宜」买单，品牌溢价空间被压缩。真正值得关注的是价值投入是否带来客流质量与复购，而非仅靠降价换量；若以牺牲毛利与品牌资产换增长，长期生意逻辑存疑。零售商自有品牌与价格架构正成为竞争主轴，需持续监测份额迁移与消费者价格锚点变化。

insights.title: Caregiver and educator preferences for school meal services in special schools for students with physical disabilities: A conjoint study of stakeholder role and mealtime difficulty severity
insights.summary: 该研究以联合分析考察身体残疾特殊学校中照护者与教育者对校餐服务的偏好，并检验利益相关者角色与进餐困难严重程度如何调节偏好结构。它把校餐从营养供给问题重构为多方利益相关者的服务设计问题，对理解特殊人群的餐饮决策与产品服务配置具有方法学与实务价值。
insights.core: 核心论点是：校餐偏好并非单一群体的一致排序，而随利益相关者角色与进餐困难严重程度系统性分化；联合分析量化了各服务属性的相对权重，说明同一服务方案在不同角色与难度情境下价值不同，因而统一配置难以最优。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：特殊人群餐饮中"代理偏好"与"直接感知"在多大程度上一致，以及困难程度作为调节变量是否应成为常态分层维度；应建立跨角色、跨严重程度的偏好稳定性监测视角，而非一次性测评。
insights.viewCMI: 从CMI看，此文把"校餐"从采购与营养议题转为多利益相关者决策结构：照护者、教育者与最终使用者诉求不一致，且随困难程度分层。这折射出特殊人群餐饮是典型的"代理决策"市场——付费者、照护者与使用者分离，偏好不可合并。长期启发是：面向特殊需求人群的产品与服务，需按角色与情境细分而非按人群整体定义，渠道与沟通对象应区分决策者与使用者。

insights.title: Exploring Italian consumer perceptions and acceptance of innovative foods and food technologies: insights from a national survey
insights.summary: 该研究基于意大利全国性调查，考察消费者对创新食品及食品技术的感知与接受度。核心在于揭示接受度并非单一态度，而受技术类型、感知收益与风险、信任与信息框架共同塑造；为创新食品的市场沟通与感官—消费者研究提供全国样本证据。
insights.core: 中心论点是：消费者对创新食品与技术的接受度是分技术类型、分情境的，不能以笼统「创新友好/抗拒」概括；全国样本显示感知收益、风险与信任是分化接受的关键，这决定创新能否跨越消费者心理门槛。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：消费者对创新食品的接受是稳定的态度倾向，还是随技术类型与信息框架漂移的情境判断？应建立跨技术类别的接受度监测视角，并持续检验感官体验与消费者预期之间的落差如何反向塑造信任。
insights.viewCMI: 从CMI看，全国调查的价值不在接受度高低本身，而在揭示创新食品的市场合法性取决于消费者对技术—收益—风险的认知结构，而非产品功能。这折射出创新供给与消费者信任之间的结构性错配：技术叙事越强，信任成本越高。长期启发是，创新食品的商业化应先建立可被消费者理解的收益框架与风险沟通秩序，而非以技术先进性替代市场教育。
insights.viewSensory: 从感官研究看，该文提醒创新食品的接受度不能只归因于技术态度，感官预期与真实感官体验的落差是关键中介：消费者对「创新」的想象会先于品尝形成预期，进而影响接受。方法上，全国调查擅长态度分层，但难以捕捉感官属性与感知机制；长期需把描述性/偏爱性测评与态度调查对接，验证感官体验能否兑现技术承诺。

insights.title: From structure to function: a review of absorption mechanisms and chronic metabolic disease interventions of phospholipid-bound omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids
insights.summary: 该综述发表于 Frontiers in Nutrition，系统梳理了磷脂结合型 omega-3 多不饱和脂肪酸（如磷脂酰胆碱-DHA/EPA）的吸收机制及其对慢性代谢疾病的干预证据，比较其与甘油三酯型、乙酯型在生物利用度与代谢路径上的差异，并讨论结构-功能关系。其价值在于把「载体形式」确立为影响 n-3 功效的关键变量，为配方设计与功效验证提供机制层面的依据。

insights.core: 核心论点是：omega-3 的健康效应不只取决于摄入量，更取决于其分子载体形式——磷脂结构可能改变肠内胶束化、淋巴转运与组织递送效率，从而影响代谢疾病干预效果。其重要性在于把「结构—吸收—功能」链条显性化，提示以总 EPA+DHA 计量评价产品与证据的范式存在系统性偏差。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：以总 EPA+DHA 计量评价功效的假设是否仍成立？载体结构差异应如何纳入功效证据分级？建议建立「载体形式—吸收效率—感官可接受性」三位一体的长期监测视角，而非依赖单次试验结论。
insights.viewSensory: 对感官研究而言，磷脂载体不是纯药理学议题：它同时改变氧化稳定性、乳化与口感表现，并可能带来腥味释放与质构差异，直接影响可接受性。本文提示感官评价需与生物利用度并列，而非事后补救；长期看，含脂功能性食品应将「感知—吸收」视为同一设计问题，建立跨学科的属性—功效联合表征框架，避免高功效配方因感官缺陷在真实消费场景中失效。

insights.title: Dietary deterioration from midlife to late life, intrinsic capacity decline, and mortality: a 10-year CLHLS study
insights.summary: 基于中国老年健康影响因素跟踪调查（CLHLS）十年数据，研究考察中年至老年阶段膳食质量恶化与内在能力（intrinsic capacity）衰退及死亡率的关联，将营养暴露与功能状态轨迹纳入同一纵向框架，提示膳食劣化可能是能力衰退的可干预前因。

insights.core: 中心论点是膳食质量随增龄的恶化并非无害的背景变化，而与内在能力衰退和死亡风险同向演进；其价值在于把营养从单点摄入指标转为贯穿中老年的可追踪暴露，为功能衰退的早期识别提供上游线索，但观察性设计难以确立因果。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：感官可接受性在多大程度上中介了膳食质量与能力衰退的关联？应建立跨年龄段的感官功能与食物选择纵向监测视角，检验「适口性优先」是否比「营养宣教」更能改变老年膳食轨迹。
insights.viewSensory: 该文的感官相关性在于：膳食质量测量本质上依赖食物与膳食的感官可接受性——滋味、质地、香气与咀嚼吞咽体验，会随味觉嗅觉敏感度下降、牙列与唾液功能变化而改变，进而驱动老年人食物选择收窄。这提示感官研究需从「青年偏好测试」扩展到全生命周期的感知衰退轨迹，把感官阈值、质地适配与适口性纳入老年食品设计范式，而非仅以营养强化为终点。

insights.title: A community-based betel nut dependence screening questionnaire developed with the modified Delphi method
insights.summary: 该研究采用改良德尔菲法，汇集专家意见构建了一套社区场景下的槟榔依赖筛查问卷，发表于 Frontiers in Nutrition。它把槟榔依赖的识别从临床或实验室场景下沉到社区自评工具，为高流行地区的早期筛查与干预提供了可操作的测量载体。

insights.core: 核心论点是槟榔依赖可在社区层面用结构化问卷可靠筛查，方法学上以改良德尔菲法保证专家共识与内容效度。其重要性在于填补了槟榔依赖缺乏轻量化、可推广筛查工具的空白，使依赖识别前移至日常场景。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：依赖量表能否与感官属性图谱建立可验证的映射，识别哪些感知维度是依赖形成的驱动因子；以及跨文化、跨人群的测量等值性是否需要重新验证。
insights.viewSensory: 从感官研究看，槟榔依赖的核心机制涉及口腔刺激感、涩感、香气与生理唤起等复合感知体验，问卷将主观依赖转化为可测量的条目，实质是把感官—情绪—行为链条工具化。这折射出感官评价正从描述性、偏爱性测评向「感知驱动的健康风险测量」延伸，长期看提示感官研究者需关注成瘾性品类中感知属性与依赖形成的耦合，而非仅停留在喜好度层面。

insights.title: Front-of-package ultraprocessed warning labels: a randomized controlled trial with Chilean parents
insights.summary: 该研究以智利家长为对象开展随机对照试验，检验包装正面超加工食品警示标签的效果。作为感官研究主题，其核心在于标签这一外部视觉与认知线索如何影响消费者对产品的感知判断与选择倾向，而非产品自身风味质地。结果为评估警示标签作为感官信息干预手段的有效性提供因果证据。

insights.core: 中心论点是：包装正面超加工警示标签能否改变家长的感知与选择行为，需用随机对照试验而非相关性调查来验证。其价值在于把标签从营销装饰转为可检验的感官—认知干预变量，为标签设计的感知效果提供因果证据基础。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：标签类外部线索对感官预期与实际体验落差的影响是否稳定可复现；应建立「信息线索—预期—感知—接受度」的长期监测框架，而非依赖单次试验结论。
insights.viewSensory: 从感官研究看，警示标签属于外部线索，通过认知预期而非口腔感知影响产品评价，触及「标签—预期—感知」链条。其启示是：感官测评需区分产品内在属性与包装信息带来的期望效应，偏爱性测试若忽略标签情境可能高估或低估真实接受度。长期应追问：警示强度如何改变感官期待与复购间的落差，以及不同感官品类对警示线索的敏感度差异。

insights.title: Editorial: Lipids in foods and nutrition: innovative analytical and biochemical insights
insights.summary: Frontiers in Nutrition 的社论聚焦食品与营养中的脂质，强调创新分析与生化视角，属方法学与机制层面的学术进展，而非消费趋势或市场报告。其价值在于为脂质相关感官属性（风味释放、口感、氧化劣变）提供更精细的测量与机理基础，间接影响产品设计与品质评价，但本身不构成市场或消费者结论。

insights.core: 中心论点是脂质研究需借助更先进的分析与生化手段，才能把脂质组成、氧化与代谢机制讲清楚；其重要性在于为食品品质与营养评价提供更可靠的方法基础，而非给出具体数据或消费结论。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：脂质组成与氧化状态如何稳定映射到具体感官属性，而非笼统的“油腻感”？应建立脂质—感知关联的长期监测视角，并检验现有感官描述词是否足以捕捉脂质差异。
insights.viewSensory: 从感官研究看，该社论指向脂质这一常被低估的感官基底：脂质既承载风味物质的分配与释放，又通过氧化与质构影响口感与异味感知。更精细的分析与生化视角，意味着感官评价可更早、更准地定位脂质相关的感知差异，把描述性测评与仪器数据更紧密地对应。长期启发是：脂质感官不应只停留在整体喜好判断，而应建立成分—机制—感知的可追溯链条，使配方调整与货架期感官劣变有据可依。

insights.title: Structural characterization and prebiotic activity of a novel polysaccharide from rice bran
insights.summary: 《Frontiers in Nutrition》刊发研究，从米糠中分离并结构表征了一种新型多糖，并验证其体外/体内益生元活性。该工作属营养科学与功能性配料基础研究，为米糠副产物高值化及益生元候选物开发提供依据，但尚未涉及感官属性或消费者测试。

insights.core: 核心论点是米糠来源新型多糖具备可被表征的化学结构与益生元活性，关键支撑为结构解析与益生元活性评价；其意义在于把米糠从低值副产物推向功能性配料候选，为益生元原料多元化提供科学基础，但距离产品化与感官验证仍远。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：益生元功效证据与感官可接受性之间的权衡应如何前置评估？米糠等副产物高值化路径中，结构表征、功效验证与感官设计能否形成并行而非串行的研发框架，是需要持续监测的方向。
insights.viewSensory: 从感官研究视角看，此文属上游原料科学，未触及风味、质地、香气及感知机制，也未做描述性或偏爱性测评。其潜在感官含义在于：多糖类配料进入食品基质后可能改变黏度、口感与风味释放，益生元活性与感官可接受性常存在张力。长期启发是功能性配料开发应尽早把感官表征纳入链条，避免「结构—活性」成立却在口感上失败。

insights.title: Exploring the feasibility and acceptability of sensory-adapted menus for adolescents with autism spectrum disorder in a school canteen: the AUT-MENU pilot study
insights.summary: 该试点研究在学校食堂场景中检验为自闭症谱系青少年设计感官适配菜单的可行性与可接受性，属感官研究范畴，将感官测评方法从实验室与常规人群拓展至神经多样性群体，为公共餐饮环境的产品感官设计提供初步证据。

insights.core: 研究核心在于：感官适配菜单在真实学校食堂环境中对自闭症青少年是否可执行、可接受；其价值不在结论强弱，而在把「感官差异」从个体偏好问题转为菜单与就餐环境的设计变量，提示感官研究需纳入神经多样性人群。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：现有感官测评工具对神经多样性人群是否具备构念效度？「可接受性」在临床与餐饮场景中应如何定义与测量？应建立跨人群的感官偏好基线监测，而非以单次试点结论替代结构性判断。
insights.viewSensory: 该研究把感官研究的方法论边界推向神经多样性人群：传统描述性与偏爱性测评多以典型感知者为基础，而自闭症群体在质地、气味、混合度上的感知阈值与厌恶反应可能显著不同，单一「平均偏好」模型会系统性遗漏这部分需求。其长期启发是感官设计应从「为多数人优化」转向「为感知差异分层设计」，并建立针对特殊人群的测评工具与接受度指标，而非简单套用常规量表。

insights.title: Editorial: Phytochemicals: molecular mechanisms for anti-aging and aging-related diseases
insights.summary: 《Frontiers in Nutrition》刊发社论，聚焦植物化学物在抗衰老及衰老相关疾病中的分子机制，属基础营养与机理研究，未涉及消费者行为、市场或产品感官属性测评。其对行业的直接意义在于为功能性配料与抗衰概念提供机理层面的证据积累。

insights.core: 中心论点是植物化学物的抗衰作用需落到可验证的分子通路而非笼统的「天然即有效」；社论以机制证据为组织线索，强调从体外与通路层面建立因果链条。其重要性在于为后续人群干预与功效声称奠定基础，但社论本身不构成消费端或感官端的结论。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：植物化学物的分子机制证据能否与感官接受度、人群有效剂量形成同一条证据链？应建立对「机理热度—产品可感知性—功效声称合规」三者错配的持续监测视角，而非追逐单一机制热点。
insights.viewSensory: 从感官研究视角看，本文属机理层证据，与风味、质地、香气等感官属性及描述性/偏爱性测评方法无直接交集，故不构成感官范式变化。但其长期启发在于：抗衰类功能性配料常伴随苦涩、异味与口感负担，机制有效性若无法在真实基质中保持可感知的接受度，价值将被感官门槛稀释。值得追问的是，机理证据如何与感官接受度、消费者感知阈值形成可对接的证据链，而非各自独立推进。

insights.summary: 一项体外（ex vivo）研究显示，低聚半乳糖（GOS）对儿童肠道菌群、代谢组与屏障功能呈剂量依赖改善，发表于 Frontiers in Nutrition。该研究属营养与肠道生理范畴，未涉及产品感官属性或消费者行为测量，对感官研究与CMI的直接外推有限。

insights.core: 核心论点是GOS对儿童肠道微生态与屏障功能的益处具有剂量依赖性，证据来自体外菌群/代谢组与屏障指标，而非人群消费或感官测评。其价值在于为益生元配方剂量设计提供机制层面的参考，但外推至真实消费与感官体验仍需人体与行为数据。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：功能成分的「有效剂量」与「可接受感官剂量」之间是否存在系统性缺口？应建立将肠道生理指标、感官属性与真实摄入行为并列监测的长期框架，检验体外机制结论在人群感官与接受度上的可迁移性。
insights.viewSensory: 从感官研究视角看，该文并未触及风味、质地、香气等感官属性或偏爱性测评，其相关性是间接的：GOS作为益生元，剂量提升往往伴随甜味、黏度与口感变化，也可能带来胀气等体感不适，构成配方感官设计的现实约束。它提示感官研究应把「功能性剂量」纳入产品设计变量，关注功能成分在有效剂量下的感官代价与消费者感知阈值，而非仅做孤立的描述性分析。

insights.title: The cardiometabolic transition in Mexico: cohort-level evidence from the ENNVIH, 2002–2009
insights.summary: 该文基于墨西哥ENNVIH队列2002–2009年数据，追踪同一人群心血管代谢指标随时间的转变，属流行病学与营养转变研究。其价值在于用队列证据揭示饮食结构变化与代谢风险的关联，为食品营养设计与消费趋势提供人群层面的背景参照。

insights.core: 中心论点是墨西哥正经历心血管代谢转变，且该转变需在个体生命周期内以队列视角观察，而非横截面比较。队列证据显示代谢风险随年龄与饮食环境累积，提示营养干预与产品设计应面向长期暴露而非单时点。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：感官喜好是否随代谢风险累积而系统性漂移？应建立人群层面的感官偏好与营养暴露纵向监测，检验「减害配方」的长期接受度假设，而非依赖单次测评结论。
insights.viewSensory: 从感官研究看，本文虽非感官测评，却间接提示产品感官设计与营养目标之间的张力：减糖减盐减脂往往改变风味、质地与香气，进而影响依从性。长期启发是，感官研究需把「长期可接受性」而非单次喜好作为核心指标，建立跨年份的感官—营养联合追踪，理解口味偏好如何随代谢状态与年龄迁移，避免配方优化只停留在短期愉悦。

insights.core: 核心在于将运动视为调节食物奖赏的干预变量，而非仅能量消耗手段；其效力与机制（奖赏回路、食欲控制）尚需更稳健证据。更正事件本身说明该交叉领域结论仍在演进，提示对『运动改变想吃什么、多想吃』的推断应保持谨慎。
insights.action: 值得长期追问：食物奖赏的测量能否区分感官享乐与代谢驱动的动机？不同体重与运动状态下，偏好测试的稳定性边界在哪？应建立跨状态的纵向感官—行为监测视角，而非单点横断结论。
insights.viewSensory: 食物奖赏是感官享乐与摄入动机的交叉点，本文把运动作为可调节该奖赏的变量，暗示感官偏好并非固定，可能随生理状态与行为干预漂移。这对感官测评提出方法论挑战：偏爱性测试若脱离运动、体重与代谢状态，结论的可迁移性存疑。长期看，感官研究或需把『状态依赖的享乐反应』纳入设计，而非只测静态偏好。

readings.title: Trump wants an immigration deal. He could start with caregivers.
readings.summary: Unlike projecting how many jobs AI may eliminate over the next 10 years, or what a country’s birth rate might look like, there’s far less de
body: Life Trump wants an immigration deal. He could start with caregivers. There’s already bipartisan interest in trying to solve one of America’s biggest eldercare problems. by Rachel Cohen Booth Updated Nov 9, 2026, 5:55 PM UTC Gift Eleanor Davis for Vox Rachel Cohen Booth is a senior policy correspondent for Vox covering social policy. She focuses on housing, schools, homelessness, childcare, and abortion rights, and has been reporting on these issues for the last 15 years. Unlike projecting how many jobs AI may eliminate over the next 10 years, or what a country’s birth rate might look like, there’s far less debate among policymakers about how large America’s older population will be in a decade’s time, and how many of them are likely to need direct care for disabilities. By 2036, as the baby boomers continue to retire, the US population 65 and older is expected to grow from 65.6 million to 77.5 million people, according to the Congressional Budget Office. The number of people 85 and older is also expected to nearly double in that time, from 6.8 million to 11.1 million. The question of whether the United States will have enough direct care workers — an umbrella term that refers to home health aides, personal care aides, and nursing assistants — looms large. These are workers, primarily women, who help older adults and people with disabilities bathe, dress, eat, take their medication, and generally get through a day, either in a nursing home or in someone’s own home. It’s a massive, often ignored workforce (the American Community Survey estimates there were 3.62 million of them in 2024) and it’s paid for largely by Medicaid, the joint federal-state health insurance program that most people associate with coverage for impoverished Americans but which is actually the dominant payer for long-term care in this country. By 2036 the US will need 625,000 to 1.3 million more direct care workers, and policymakers across the aisle agree the demand is real and coming. Three bipartisan-friendly proposals — the Dignity Act, the Careworker Visa Act, and a Brookings caregiving visa — would bring in immigrant caregivers with built-in protections learned from past programs. With around 40 cosponsors from both parties and Problem Solvers Caucus backing, the Dignity Act has more bipartisan traction than most immigration bills in years. Trump has also expressed new openness to immigration reform. Depending on which researcher you ask, the US will need somewhere between 625,000 and 1.3 million additional direct care workers over the next decade to keep pace with the growing number of older and disabled Americans — and that’s just to maintain today’s level of care as the population ages, not to fix the shortage that already exists. If you’ve talked to anyone currently trying to coordinate long-term care, you probably already know the country is understaffed as it is. To close the gap, policy experts say the United States should bring more immigrants into a sector that’s already about one-third immigrant , while also protecting the roughly 12 percent of current direct care workers who are noncitizens, some of them undocumented. PHI, a national nonprofit that researches and advocates for the direct care workforce, projects 9.6 million direct care job openings between 2025 and 2035, the bulk of which will come from existing workers changing fields, retiring, or otherwise leaving the workforce. “We can’t do it with the current US-born workforce,” Amy Robins, the senior director of policy at PHI, told me. “We need to have mechanisms where people can come into this country and do this work.” Immigration reform has felt politically impossible in Washington for years, but after the brutal defeat Republicans suffered in the midterms, there’s a suddenly a much stronger case that this corner of the fight is different. Days after the election, President Donald Trump gave an interview saying his deportation policy was “too tough” and he’d be open to some sort of immigration reform deal to protect workers. In September 2025, Sens. Kevin Cramer (R-ND) and Dick Durbin (D-IL) reintroduced a bill to recover green cards that went unused in earlier years and redirect them to nurses and doctors. Coordinating care for older adults is a problem that reaches families in every corner of the country, and even comfortable households wonder whether they can secure a dignified life for an aging parent, or, eventually, for themselves. With family caregivers growing in number and nursing homes turning residents away because they can’t find staff, caregiving may be the one corner of immigration policy Congress is actually willing to fix. Over the last year or so, three different proposals have emerged that suggest that caregiving is the immigration battle Washington is finally ready to fight. In July 2025, Reps. María Elvira Salazar (R-FL) and Veronica Escobar (D-TX) introduced the Dignity Act , which pairs tougher border enforcement with legal status for undocumented immigrants who’ve been in the country since before 2021. It also offers permanent residency for Dreamers and a handful of green card reforms. Salazar herself has pitched the bill partly as a remedy for the same aging-population squeeze driving the caregiver shortage, and eldercare groups such as LeadingAge and the American Seniors Housing Association have thrown their support behind it . The legislation rests on an idea at the center of the caregiving political fight, which is that immigration enforcement alone won’t get the US the labor it needs. Since then, the Dignity Act has gathered around 40 cosponsors, split nearly down the middle between the parties, and this spring it won the endorsement of the Problem Solvers Caucus, a group of roughly 60 members whose mandate is passing legislation both sides can live with. Following Trump’s recent comments that he’d be open to an immigration deal, Salazar praised him on X, urging him to throw his weight behind the Dignity Act. “You can surpass Reagan’s legacy by delivering a historic immigration reform,” she posted. “This is your moment.” There are other ideas on the table, too. Over the summer, Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-NM) introduced the Careworker Visa Act , a bill that would create a new temporary visa allowing up to 100,000 immigrants a year to work in childcare, eldercare, and home-based disability care. It would also let some immigrants already living in the US obtain work authorization through the program and give participating workers a pathway to permanent residency. “We all know that immigrants are already taking on these jobs in large numbers,” Vasquez told me. “One of the conversations we’re having amongst the Democratic coalition is how to craft meaningful immigration-related legislation that can be bipartisan on a couple specific issues. And certainly this bill rises to the very top of that conversation.” And the most recent entry came in September, from Tara Watson, an economist at the Brookings Institution. In a new caregiving visa proposal , she offers the idea of a visa open to immigrants with at least two years of direct care experience who want to come to the US to work as home health aides, personal care aides, or nursing assistants. It would start at 30,000 visas a year before rising to 65,000 after three years, and employers would have to pay above-market wages and provide health insurance. Neither of the two dedicated caregiving visa proposals is starting from scratch. In 1999, Congress created a visa for nurses to work in understaffed hospitals, but the process had such strict eligibility rules that fewer than 15 hospitals nationwide ever qualified to use it. And it was burdensome for qualifying workers, too: If a nurse ever wanted to switch their hospital, they had to start their visa certification process all over again. Over the course of a decade, barely a thousand visas were ever issued, and lawmakers let the program expire in 2009. Other countries have gone the opposite direction. The UK made care workers eligible for its Health and Care Worker visa in 2022 , and the numbers took off almost immediately, with 106,000 visas granted in 2023 alone. But exploitation was rampant. Some contracts required workers to repay thousands of pounds to their employer if they left before their visa term was up — one worker’s contract demanded more than 11,000 British pounds — which made leaving a bad job financially impossible for people who’d often already gone into debt just to get the job in the first place. More than 43,000 workers were affected when their employers’ sponsor licenses were revoked amid widespread reports of exploitation. The UK ended overseas recruitment for care workers in 2025, though the broader Health and Care Worker visa remains in place. Both experiments reflected the fact that workers often had no way out, no matter how poorly an employer behaved. Watson and Vasquez say they kept that front of mind when crafting their proposals, both of which allow workers to switch jobs rather than staying locked to whoever sponsored them. “You really do see this tension — the more you try to make sure the workers are protected, the more onerous it becomes for the employers,” Watson told me. “You’re choosing between scale and some of those restrictions. I’m trying to hit somewhat of a middle ground.” Vasquez pointed to the H-2A visa program for farmworkers, which he said has also had real, ongoing problems with employers abusing the system. “Anytime that we are creating new programs for immigrant workers in which their job status depends on them achieving legal status, we should always be aware that there may be bad folks that are seeking to abuse that system,” he told me. “That’s going to require some thoughtful support for the Department of Labor for enforcement of laws just like this.” These federal ideas build on top of a patchwork of state-level attempts to raise direct care wages in order to incentivize more people living here to enter and stay in the field. Yet for all the state mandates, bonuses, and training programs, care programs are usually among the first casualties when money gets tight. And even in states that have pulled off real wage increases, inflation has frequently swallowed those gains before they could do much to close the gap. LeadingAge, which represents nonprofit nursing homes, assisted living communities, and home care agencies, says no single state’s budget can fix this. Linda Couch, the organization’s senior vice president of policy, says states are now facing significant cuts to their Medicaid funding under last year’s federal budget law, which will squeeze what providers can pay their staff. “Federal policymakers hold a lot of the cards for systemic change to meet the needs of older adults,” Couch told me. “Without action to secure immigration reform and reverse Medicaid cuts, we’re putting access to aging services at risk for older adults across the country.” LeadingAge’s members are already feeling this. Couch said one of its Massachusetts members, Hebrew SeniorLife, had to let go of nearly 40 Haitian workers this year after their Temporary Protected Status ended, some of whom had worked there for more than a decade. A Florida provider lost 10 workers from Cuba and Haiti after a humanitarian parole program shut down . Congressional Republicans to date have primarily rallied around tax credits and retirement protections for the nation’s 63 million family caregivers . Robins of PHI, though, doesn’t see the two approaches as inherently at odds. “There are way more family caregivers in this country than there are direct care workers, and that will always be true,” she told me. It’s a “yes, and” when it comes to supporting family caregivers, she said, and direct care workers are a “fundamental way that we support family caregivers who are taking on tremendous care responsibilities in our country right now.” A paid home health aide coming a few days a week, in other words, can be what lets a daughter or spouse keep working, or just get a full night’s sleep, while still caring for a parent at home. The population who will need this care by 2036 is already here. It may not be much, but caregiving, as Watson said, is “low-hanging fruit, if there is any low-hanging fruit.” In an immigration debate this stuck, that counts for something. 特朗普想要达成一项移民协议。他可以从照护者入手。两党已有兴趣尝试解决美国最大的养老难题之一。作者：Rachel Cohen Booth 更新时间：2026年11月9日，下午5:55 UTC 赠予 Eleanor Davis for Vox Rachel Cohen Booth 是 Vox 的高级政策记者，报道社会政策。她专注于住房、学校、无家可归、儿童照护和堕胎权等议题，过去15年来一直在报道这些问题。与预测AI在未来10年可能消灭多少工作岗位、或一个国家出生率会是什么样子不同，政策制定者对于美国十年后老年人口规模会有多大、其中有多少人可能需要针对残障的直接照护，争论要少得多。根据美国国会预算办公室的数据，到2036年，随着婴儿潮一代持续退休，美国65岁及以上人口预计将从6560万增至7750万。同期，85岁及以上人口预计也将几乎翻倍，从680万增至1110万。美国是否有足够的直接照护工作者——这是一个统称，指家庭健康助理、个人护理助理和护理助理——这个问题日益凸显。这些工作者主要是女性，她们帮助老年人和残障人士洗澡、穿衣、进食、服药，并 generally 度过一天，工作场所要么是养老院，要么是在某人自己的家中。这是一个庞大却常被忽视的劳动力群体（美国社区调查估计2024年有362万人），其薪酬主要由医疗补助计划支付。医疗补助是联邦与州联合的健康保险项目，大多数人将其与贫困美国人的保险覆盖联系在一起，但它实际上是美国长期照护的主要支付方。到2036年，美国将需要新增62.5万至130万名直接照护工作者，两党政策制定者都认同这一需求真实存在且即将到来。三项两党友好的提案——《尊严法案》、《照护工作者签证法案》以及布鲁金斯学会的照护签证——将引入移民照护者，并附带从以往项目中吸取教训而设计的保障措施。《尊严法案》拥有约40名两党联署人和问题解决者党团的背书，其两党支持力度超过多年来大多数移民法案。特朗普也表达了对移民改革的新开放态度。取决于你问哪位研究者，美国在未来十年将需要新增62.5万至130万名直接照护工作者，才能跟上日益增长的老年和残障美国人数量——而这仅仅是在人口老龄化过程中维持当今的照护水平，并非解决已经存在的短缺。如果你和任何目前正试图

##段落
要协调长期护理，你大概已经知道这个国家本就人手不足。为了填补缺口，政策专家表示，美国应当让更多移民进入这个本已有约三分之一是移民的行业，同时保护目前约12%的直接护理工作者中的非公民，其中一些人还是无证移民。PHI是一家研究并倡导直接护理劳动力的全国性非营利组织，它预计2025年至2035年间将有960万个直接护理职位空缺，其中大部分将来自现有工作者转行、退休或以其他方式离开劳动力队伍。“靠目前美国本土的劳动力，我们做不到，”PHI政策高级主管艾米·罗宾斯对我说。“我们需要有机制让人们能够来到这个国家从事这项工作。”多年来，移民改革在华盛顿在政治上一直被认为不可能，但在共和党于中期选举中惨败之后，突然有了更有力的理由认为，这场斗争的这一角有所不同。选举几天后，唐纳德·特朗普总统在接受采访时说，他的驱逐政策“太严厉”，他愿意接受某种移民改革协议以保护工人。2025年9月，参议员凯文·克拉默（北达科他州共和党）和迪克·德宾（伊利诺伊州民主党）重新提出一项法案，拟收回早年未使用的绿卡，并将其转给护士和医生。协调老年人的护理是一个触及全国每个角落家庭的问题，即便是富裕家庭也想知道，他们能否为年迈的父母、或最终为自己争取有尊严的生活。随着家庭照护者人数增加，而养老院因找不到员工而拒收住户，照护或许正是国会真正愿意修复的移民政策一角。在过去一年左右的时间里，出现了三项不同的提案，表明照护正是华盛顿终于准备打的移民之战。2025年7月，众议员玛丽亚·埃尔维拉·萨拉查（佛罗里达州共和党）和维罗妮卡·埃斯科巴（得克萨斯州民主党）提出了《尊严法案》，该法案将更严格的边境执法与为2021年之前已在该国的无证移民提供合法身份相结合。它还为“梦想生”提供永久居留权，并包含若干绿卡改革。萨拉查本人曾部分地将该法案宣传为对同样推动照护者短缺的老龄化人口压力的补救，而LeadingAge和美国老年人住房协会等养老团体已表示支持。该立法基于照护政治斗争核心的一个理念，即仅靠移民执法无法让美国获得所需的劳动力。自那以后，《尊严法案》已获得

##段落
该法案已获得约40位共同提案人支持，两党分布几乎各占一半，并于今年春天赢得了“问题解决者党团”的背书——该党团约有60名成员，其宗旨是推动两党都能接受的立法。在特朗普最近表示愿意接受移民协议后，萨拉萨尔在X上称赞了他，并敦促他全力支持《尊严法案》。“你可以通过推动历史性的移民改革来超越里根的遗产，”她发文写道，“这是你的时刻。”桌面上还有其他方案。今年夏天，众议员加布·巴斯克斯（新墨西哥州民主党人）提出了《护理工作者签证法案》，该法案将设立一种新的临时签证，每年允许多达10万名移民从事儿童保育、养老护理和居家残障护理工作。该法案还将允许部分已在美国居住的移民通过该计划获得工作许可，并为参与计划的工作者提供获得永久居留权的途径。“我们都知道，移民已经在大量从事这些工作，”巴斯克斯告诉我。“我们在民主党联盟内部进行的讨论之一，是如何在几个具体议题上制定能够获得两党支持的、有意义的移民相关立法。毫无疑问，这项法案在讨论中位居最前列。”最新的方案出现在9月，来自布鲁金斯学会的经济学家塔拉·沃森。在一项新的护理签证提案中，她提出了一种签证构想，面向拥有至少两年直接护理经验、希望来美国从事家庭健康助理、个人护理助理或护理助理工作的移民。该签证初始为每年3万份，三年后增至6.5万份，雇主须支付高于市场水平的工资并提供医疗保险。两项专门的护理签证提案都不是从零开始。1999年，国会为护士在人手不足的医院工作设立了一种签证，但资格规定极为严格，全国仅有不到15家医院曾有资格使用。而且对符合条件的工作者来说负担也很重：如果护士想换医院，就必须重新走一遍签证认证流程。十年间，发放的签证 barely 超过一千份，议员们于2009年让该计划到期终止。其他国家则走了相反的方向。英国于2022年将护理工作者纳入其“健康与护理工作者签证”的适用范围，签证数量几乎立即激增，仅2023年就发放了10.6万份。但剥削现象十分猖獗。一些合同要求工作者如果在签证到期前离职，须向雇主偿还数千英镑——一名工作者的合同要求偿还超过1.1万英镑——

##段落
这使得人们即便想离开一份糟糕的工作，在经济上也几乎不可能——而这些人往往一开始就是为了得到这份工作才背上了债务。当雇主的担保执照被吊销时，超过4.3万名工人受到影响，与此同时，关于剥削的报道广泛存在。英国于2025年终止了护理人员的海外招聘，不过更广泛的“健康与护理工作者”签证仍然保留。这两项试验都反映出同一个事实：无论雇主的行为多么恶劣，工人往往无路可退。沃森和巴斯克斯表示，他们在制定提案时始终牢记这一点，两人的方案都允许工人更换工作，而不是被牢牢绑定在担保他们的雇主身上。沃森对我说：“你确实能看到这种张力——你越是努力确保工人受到保护，对雇主来说负担就越沉重。你是在规模和某些限制之间做取舍。我试图找到一个折中点。”巴斯克斯提到了针对农场工人的H-2A签证项目，他说该项目同样长期存在雇主滥用制度的真实问题。他对我说：“每当我们为移民工人创建新项目、而他们的工作身份取决于能否获得合法身份时，我们都应该始终意识到，可能会有不怀好意的人试图滥用这一制度。这就需要为劳工部提供一些周到的支持，以执行这样的法律。”这些联邦层面的构想建立在各州零散尝试的基础之上——各州试图提高直接护理工资，以激励更多本地居民进入并留在这个行业。然而，尽管有各种州级强制规定、奖金和培训项目，一旦资金紧张，护理项目通常是最先受到冲击的。即便在那些确实实现了工资增长的州，通胀也往往在这些增长来得及缩小差距之前就将其吞噬殆尽。代表非营利养老院、辅助生活社区和居家护理机构的LeadingAge表示，没有任何一个州的预算能解决这个问题。该组织负责政策的高级副总裁琳达·库奇表示，根据去年的联邦预算法，各州目前面临医疗补助资金的大幅削减，这将挤压服务提供者支付员工薪酬的能力。库奇对我说：“联邦政策制定者掌握着实现系统性变革以满足老年人需求的大部分主动权。如果不采取行动推进移民改革、扭转医疗补助削减，我们就在让全国老年人获得养老服务的渠道面临风险。”LeadingAge的成员已经感受到了这一点。库奇说，其马萨诸塞州成员之一Hebrew SeniorLife今年不得不在近40名海地工人的临时保护身份到期后将其解雇，其中一些人……

##段落
她在那裡工作了十多年。佛羅里達州一家服務機構在人道主義假釋計劃終止後，失去了10名來自古巴和海地的員工。迄今為止，國會共和黨人主要圍繞稅收抵免和退休保障來爭取全國6300萬家庭照護者的支持。不過，PHI的羅賓斯並不認為這兩種做法本質上相互對立。她對我說：「這個國家的家庭照護者遠多於直接照護工作者，而且這一點永遠都會如此。」她說，在支持家庭照護者這件事上，這是「是的，而且」的關係，而直接照護工作者是「我們支持家庭照護者的根本方式，這些家庭照護者目前在我國承擔著巨大的照護責任」。換句話說，每週有幾天有付費的家庭健康助理上門，可以讓女兒或配偶繼續工作，或者至少能睡個整夜覺，同時仍在家中照顧父母。到2036年將需要這種照護的人群已經存在。這可能不算多，但正如沃森所說，照護工作是「低垂的果實，如果真有低垂的果實的話」。在一場如此僵持的移民辯論中，這也算是有意義的。

readings.title: China's great emissions slow-down
readings.summary: These five charts show why China's emissions are finally slowing down
body: 9 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Xiaoying You The growth of China's emissions may have virtually stopped as it races ahead with its rapid rollout of renewables. Five charts show how it reached this milestone and what lies ahead. China – the world's largest emitter of carbon dioxide (CO2) – has reached a major milestone: in the first half of 2026, less than half of the country's electricity was generated by coal for the first time in its history. Twenty years ago, these dirty black rocks were the pillar of China's economy: coal power accounted for 80% of all the electricity the country gobbled as it undertook rapid modernisation. But while the country's overall electricity demand has expanded since then, growing solar and wind power are increasingly lessening its reliance on coal power . Once China's carbon emissions peak, the global carbon emissions will likely peak, too – Yu Aiqun The result of this substantial shift is a potent signal for the country's – and the world's – effort to reach net zero: the growth of China's CO2 emissions has virtually stopped in recent years , according to one assessment. China's emissions may even have peaked in 2025 , according to another analysis – five years ahead of the country's own deadline . From solar megafarms to electric trucks, here are five charts which tell the story behind China's great emissions slowdown, how it reached this milestone and what lies ahead as it races to reach its target of net zero by 2060. China's economy has seen monumental growth over the past three decades . So have its CO2 emissions, which ballooned nearly fivefold from 1990 to 2024 . China's global share of CO2 also jumped from around 10% to more than 30% during this period, the largest global increase. China plays a "pivotal role" in the world's fight against climate change not only because it is the largest CO2 emitter, but also because its emissions have grown at the fastest rate, says Yu Aiqun, a research analyst at Global Energy Monitor (GEM), a non-profit in the US. "Once China's carbon emissions peak, global carbon emissions will likely peak, too," she says. Some believe the watershed moment is already upon China. The country's carbon emissions reached their highest level in 2024 and fell in 2025 , according to data from Climate Action Tracker (CAT), a collaborative project that assesses governments' climate actions. CAT predicts China's carbon emissions will decrease by about 18% by 2035. A separate analysis by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish think tank, found that China's CO2 emissions have remained flat or falling since March 2024, bar a small rise in early 2026. Similar trends have happened before, for example when China's government downsized steelmaking and coal power between 2014 and 2016, and during Covid-19, when lockdowns paused manufacturing and transport activity. But this time there is a fundamental difference, says Belinda Schäpe, CREA's China team lead. The rapid decline is not only driven by the shrinking output of some heavy industries, but also by China's "enormous expansion" of clean energy and growing use of electricity – instead of fossil fuels – to power machines, vehicles and devices. It is hard to say with certainty whether China has already achieved its goal to peak CO2 emissions by 2030 . Beijing's existing policy language is "ambiguous", says Lauri Myllyvirta, CREA's lead analyst. "The government has not defined what it means for emissions to have peaked – whether it refers to emissions stabilising or peaking then declining – and how this would be verified." China has yet to confirm whether its CO2 emissions have peaked, with the most recent emissions data released by the government for 2021 . What is more important, however, is whether China's emissions will drop quickly after the peak or remain at a high level, Yu says. Even a 1% reduction would have a profound impact on global climate action, she says. Under China's strong policy steer, massive wind and solar power stations have risen in the desert and vast arrays of solar panels have been mounted on rooftops . Gigantic wind turbines are harnessing the power of strong storms off the coast of China. In 2023 alone, China installed 217 gigawatts (GW) of solar panels, more than the US had installed in its entire history. It repeated this feat in 2024 and 2025. A renewable spree has prevented China from falling back onto fossil fuels, even though it needs to generate more and more electricity each year – for air-conditioning, EVs and data centres – says Norah Zhang, a climate-policy analyst at NewClimate Institute, a non-profit in Germany. The country's renewable capacity has grown at such a fast rate that wind and solar power were more than enough to cover the country's extra electricity demand each year, paving the way for the country to "squeeze coal out of its power system", she says. In July 2026, the installed capacity of solar in China even overtook coal for the first time (although it's worth noting that coal still generates far more electricity than solar, since solar typically generates less electricity per GW of capacity). As its renewable power has surged, China has struggled to store or make use of the excess solar and wind energy it generates as grids reach their limits. In the first six months of 2026, around 360 terawatt-hours (TWh) of wind and solar power – enough to power the UK for a year – was curtailed in China, according to CREA. China's challenge is now ensuring the power system can effectively use its expanding renewables capacity, Schäpe says. The country needs to reform its power market, roll out incentives and update its power infrastructure, she says. The share of China's electricity generated by coal has continued to shrink rapidly. By 2025, coal generated around 54% of its electricity and this further dipped to a historic low of 49.7% between January and June of 2026, according to China's National Energy Administration. This fall proves that adopting renewable energy is not only technically feasible but also cost-competitive, says Yao Zhe, a global policy advisor at Greenpeace East Asia. Wind and solar power made up 25% of China's power generation in the first half of the year, according to government data . Greenpeace projects this will rise to 33% by 2028 and 40% by 2030 . China's target is more conservative: it aims to generate 30% of its electricity using wind and solar by 2030. But researchers warn China still has a long way to go to kick its coal habit. For one, a falling share of coal power is not the same as a falling amount of coal power, Schäpe stresses. China generated 3.4% more coal power in the first half of 2026, compared to the same period last year, according to a joint assessment by CREA and GEM. "Coal power generation remains strong," Schäpe says. China's coal-powered fleet is also growing fast. In the first six months of this year, 30 gigawatts (GW) of new plants went into operation , the largest amount since 2016. Another 274GW is waiting to be built , which could expand the country's current coal-powered fleet by more than 20%. China views coal power as a safety net for its energy transition and a cornerstone of energy security and economic growth, Yu says. But its continuous expansion could damage the country's reputation as a global renewable leader, she says. Nevertheless, China's emissions have been able to hold stable partly due to falling emissions of the steel and cement industries driven by the collapse of the country's vast real-estate industry, Schäpe says. One of the main drivers of emissions' reductions, though, Schäpe adds, is the decline in oil consumption in transport following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the rapid electrification of this sector. China has left the world in the dust when it comes to the adoption of EVs and the impact on emissions is already starting to show. Between January and June 2026, China's fleet of electric cars, buses and trucks helped avoid the use of 36 million tonnes of oil , according to CREA – equivalent to half the UK's annual oil consumption . In July, more than six in every 10 new cars sold in China were "new-energy vehicles", a term used by the Chinese government to include pure electric, plug-in hybrids and fuel cell vehicles powered by alternative fuels like hydrogen. EV sales in China are expected to reach 14.3 million in 2026, nearly three times more than in Europe and 12 times higher than in the US, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). Buses , cars and scooters have led the EV deployment on Chinese roads over the past 15 years. Now, trucks have taken over the baton. The sales of electric trucks have grown exponentially in China over the past two years, with more than 400,000 sold in 2025 alone.   This extraordinary growth has been largely driven by the surge of electric heavy-duty trucks , says Mao Shiyue, a researcher at the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), a non-profit with headquarters in Washington DC. The government requires companies in dozens of industries to use a certain share of these trucks in transport fleets, or face production curtailments on heavily polluted days. As China's EV fleet balloons, so does the pressure facing its power grid, which needs to balance electricity supply with demand in real time. "If a large number of EVs charge their batteries at the same time, especially using rapid-charging modes, that could challenge the grid's stability," Mao says. Batteries are crucial for China's net-zero ambition: they power its fleet of EVs and store surplus electricity for later use . China is the world leader in battery energy storage systems , accounting for more than half of the global capacity by the end of 2025. These systems receive and store surplus renewable power, sending it back to the grid during periods of maximum energy demand. "They are a key component for a future grid that uses a higher and higher portion of wind and solar power," says Yang Biqing, an analyst at Ember, such as by storing daytime solar power and releasing it to the grid in the evening. For the past few years, China has required wind and solar stations to build or purchase a certain amount of energy-storage capacity to help the grid absorb the electricity they generate. This policy, coupled with the falling price of lithium batteries , has kickstarted a remarkable transition. By the end of March 2026, China had installed nearly 150GW of energy-storage capacity that used lithium batteries, more than the rest of the world combined, according to Ember. China aims to build more than 180GW of new energy-storage capacity, primarily those using batteries, by 2027. Still, China's energy-storage stations are currently severely underused, according to Ember . Boosting their usage – and by extension their profitability – will require more fundamental changes to China's power grid and power-trading system, which were designed to serve coal, Yang says. China's heavy investment in clean energy and EVs has begun to bear fruit, changing its power structure and bending its carbon emissions' trajectory in fundamental ways. But for many, a key question remains: will China's emissions rebound once more if its stagnant economy starts to pick up? As Yu says, coal is deeply embedded in all aspects of China's economy – decoupling the two is "the biggest challenge" the superpower faces in its bid to reach net zero. -- For essential climate news and hopeful developments to your inbox, sign up to the Future Earth newsletter, while The Essential List delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights twice a week. For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram . ##段落
9小时前 分享 收藏 在Google上添加为首选 Xiaoying You 随着中国大力推进可再生能源的部署，其排放量的增长可能实际上已经停止。五张图表展示了中国如何达到这一里程碑，以及未来将会如何。中国——全球最大的二氧化碳（CO2）排放国——已达成了一个重要里程碑：2026年上半年，中国历史上首次出现燃煤发电量占全国总发电量不到一半的情况。二十年前，这些肮脏的黑色石头是中国经济的支柱：在中国快速现代化的进程中，煤电占全国电力消费总量的80%。然而，尽管自那时以来中国的整体电力需求持续扩大，不断增长的太阳能和风能正日益削弱其对煤电的依赖。一旦中国的碳排放达峰，全球碳排放也很可能随之达峰——Yu Aiqun 这一重大转变的结果，对中国乃至全球实现净零排放的努力而言是一个强有力的信号：根据一项评估，近年来中国CO2排放量的增长实际上已经停止。根据另一项分析，中国的排放量甚至可能在2025年已经达峰——比中国自己设定的最后期限提前了五年。从太阳能巨型农场到电动卡车，以下五张图表讲述了中国排放大幅放缓背后的故事、中国如何达到这一里程碑，以及在力争2060年前实现净零目标的过程中未来将会如何。过去三十年间，中国经济实现了巨大增长。其CO2排放量也是如此，从1990年到2024年膨胀了近五倍。在此期间，中国在全球CO2排放中的占比也从约10%跃升至30%以上，为全球最大增幅。美国非营利组织全球能源监测（GEM）的研究分析师Yu Aiqun表示，中国在全球应对气候变化的斗争中扮演着“关键角色”，不仅因为它是最大的CO2排放国，还因为其排放增长速度最快。“一旦中国的碳排放达峰，全球碳排放也很可能随之达峰，”她说。一些人认为，这一转折点已经降临中国。根据评估各国政府气候行动的协作项目“气候行动追踪”（CAT）的数据，中国的碳排放量在2024年达到最高水平，并在2025年下降。CAT预测，到2035年中国碳排放将减少约18%。芬兰智库“能源与清洁空气研究中心”（CREA）的另一项分析发现，自2024年3月以来，中国的CO2排放量一直持平或下降，仅2026年初出现小幅上升。类似的趋势此前也曾出现，例如中国政府缩减钢铁和煤电规模时

##段落
2014年至2016年间，以及新冠疫情期间，封锁措施暂停了制造业和运输活动。但CREA中国团队负责人贝琳达·舍佩表示，这一次存在根本性差异。这一快速下降不仅源于部分重工业产出萎缩，也源于中国清洁能源的“巨量扩张”，以及越来越多地使用电力——而非化石燃料——来驱动机器、车辆和设备。很难确定中国是否已实现2030年前碳达峰的目标。CREA首席分析师劳里·米利维尔塔表示，北京现有的政策表述“含糊不清”。“政府没有界定排放达峰意味着什么——是指排放趋于稳定，还是达峰后下降——以及如何对此进行核实。”中国尚未确认其二氧化碳排放是否已达峰，政府发布的最新排放数据截至2021年。不过，于（音）表示，更重要的是中国的排放将在达峰后迅速下降，还是维持在高位。她说，即便是1%的降幅，也会对全球气候行动产生深远影响。在中国的强有力政策引导下，沙漠中建起了大规模风电和光伏电站，屋顶上安装了成片的光伏板。巨大的风力涡轮机正利用中国近海的强风暴发电。仅2023年一年，中国就新增了217吉瓦（GW）的光伏装机，超过美国有史以来的累计装机量。2024年和2025年，中国又重复了这一壮举。德国非营利机构新气候研究所的气候政策分析师诺拉·张表示，可再生能源的迅猛发展使中国免于重新依赖化石燃料，尽管中国每年需要为空调、电动汽车和数据中心发出越来越多的电力。她说，中国的可再生能源装机增速如此之快，风电和光伏发电足以覆盖每年新增的电力需求，为中国“将煤炭挤出电力系统”铺平了道路。2026年7月，中国的光伏装机容量甚至首次超过煤电（不过值得注意的是，煤电发电量仍远高于光伏，因为光伏每吉瓦装机通常发电量更少）。随着可再生能源发电激增，电网达到承载极限，中国在储存或利用多余的风电和光伏电力方面面临困难。据CREA数据，2026年上半年，中国弃风弃光约360太瓦时（TWh）——足以供英国使用一年。中国当前面临的挑战是确保电力系统能够有效利用其不断扩张的可再生能源。

##段落
Schäpe表示，产能是一方面。她指出，该国需要改革其电力市场、推出激励措施并更新电力基础设施。中国煤炭发电占比持续快速萎缩。根据中国国家能源局的数据，到2025年，煤炭发电约占其电力供应的54%，而在2026年1月至6月期间，这一比例进一步降至49.7%的历史低点。绿色和平东亚全球政策顾问姚喆表示，这一下降证明采用可再生能源不仅技术上可行，而且具有成本竞争力。根据政府数据，今年上半年风电和太阳能发电占中国发电量的25%。绿色和平预测，到2028年这一比例将升至33%，到2030年升至40%。中国的目标则更为保守：计划到2030年实现30%的电力来自风电和太阳能。但研究人员警告称，中国要戒掉煤炭依赖仍有很长的路要走。首先，Schäpe强调，煤炭发电占比下降并不等同于煤炭发电量下降。根据CREA和GEM的联合评估，2026年上半年中国煤炭发电量较去年同期增长了3.4%。"煤炭发电依然强劲，"Schäpe说。中国的煤电机组也在快速增长。今年前六个月，有30吉瓦（GW）的新建煤电厂投入运营，为2016年以来最大规模。另有274GW等待建设，这可能使该国现有煤电机组扩大20%以上。Yu表示，中国将煤电视为能源转型的安全网，以及能源安全和经济增长的基石。但她指出，煤电的持续扩张可能损害该国作为全球可再生能源领导者的声誉。不过，Schäpe表示，中国排放之所以能保持稳定，部分原因在于该国庞大的房地产行业崩溃导致钢铁和水泥行业排放下降。然而，Schäpe补充说，减排的主要驱动力之一是霍尔木兹海峡关闭后交通领域石油消费的下降，以及该行业的快速电气化。在电动汽车的普及方面，中国已将世界远远甩在身后，其对排放的影响已开始显现。根据CREA的数据，2026年1月至6月期间，中国的电动汽车、公交车和卡车车队帮助避免了3600万吨石油的使用——相当于英国年石油消费量的一半。今年7月，中国每售出10辆新车中就有超过6辆是"新能源汽车"——这是中国政府使用的术语，涵盖纯电动、插电式混合动力以及由氢等替代燃料驱动的燃料电池汽车。电动汽车销量在

##段落
根据国际能源署（IEA）的数据，预计到2026年，中国的电动汽车保有量将达到1430万辆，几乎是欧洲的三倍，是美国的12倍。过去15年里，公交车、轿车和踏板车引领了中国道路上电动汽车的普及。如今，卡车接过了接力棒。过去两年，中国电动卡车的销量呈指数级增长，仅2025年就售出超过40万辆。

##段落
总部位于华盛顿特区的非营利组织国际清洁交通委员会（ICCT）研究员毛世越表示，这一非凡增长在很大程度上是由电动重型卡车的激增所推动的。政府要求数十个行业的企业在运输车队中使用一定比例的此类卡车，否则在重污染天气将面临限产。随着中国电动汽车车队规模膨胀，其电网面临的压力也随之增大，电网需要实时平衡电力供需。“如果大量电动汽车同时充电，尤其是使用快充模式，可能会对电网稳定性构成挑战，”毛世越说。电池对于中国的净零排放目标至关重要：它们为电动汽车车队提供动力，并储存多余电力以备后用。中国在电池储能系统领域处于世界领先地位，截至2025年底占全球产能的一半以上。这些系统接收并储存多余的可再生电力，在能源需求高峰时段将其送回电网。“它们是未来电网的关键组成部分，未来电网将使用越来越高比例的风能和太阳能，”Ember分析师杨碧清表示，例如储存白天的太阳能并在夜间释放到电网。过去几年，中国要求风电和光伏电站建设或购买一定数量的储能容量，以帮助电网消纳其发出的电力。这一政策，加上锂电池价格下降，启动了一场显著的转型。据Ember数据，截至2026年3月底，中国已安装近150GW使用锂电池的储能容量，超过世界其他地区的总和。中国的目标是到2027年建成超过180GW的新型储能容量，主要是使用电池的储能。然而，据Ember称，中国储能电站目前的利用率严重不足。杨表示，提高其利用率——进而提升其盈利能力——将需要对中国的电网和电力交易系统进行更根本性的改革，这些系统最初是为服务煤炭而设计的。中国在清洁能源和电动汽车上的巨额投资已开始见效，改变了其电力结构，并使碳排放轨迹发生转变。

##段落
但在许多方面，一个关键问题依然存在：如果中国停滞的经济开始回暖，其碳排放是否会再次反弹？正如Yu所说，煤炭深深嵌入中国经济的方方面面——将两者脱钩是这个超级大国在争取实现净零排放过程中面临的“最大挑战”。

body: Good news: You can be a generous person without writing a bunch of checks. In fact, many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need. This type of giving is open to everyone.
Many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need.

Not sure where to begin? Here are six gifts of time and attention that have the strong potential to spark ripple effects that affect millions, from head of TED Chris Anderson’s new book, Infectious Generosity .

Zen master Thich Nhat Hanh taught that attention is the most precious gift we can give someone. This is where generosity starts — with a willingness to stop focusing on ourselves and to instead pay attention to someone else and their needs. From that act of connection, anything can happen.

Truth is, it can be difficult. We spend much of our time lost in our own worlds. We are often reluctant to focus on the issues that others are dealing with. So we put up shields. And that means that many of the people who could really use our attention never feel seen by us. The generosity of attention is therefore the generosity of being willing to be a little uncomfortable, to take down those shields, to give up some time, to risk coming to care about someone else.
Whether you stop and have a meaningful connection with a person in need or spend 30 minutes researching a cause you think might matter, you have already begun your generosity journey.

In our connected era, there’s a type of generosity that matters more than ever: a willingness to reach out to those with whom we disagree with. Many disputes today play out in public online. Huge audiences can become glued to online feuds. What if we could bring a satisfying resolution to more of these conflicts?

It’s hard to reach out to our critics. This is a particularly challenging form of the generosity mindset. You are sacrificing your personal comfort for the greater good of bringing people together. But if you’re successful, there’s a powerful knock-on benefit: You are helping change the tone of public discussion today. That’s a gift to all of us.
The single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.
In countless circumstances, the single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.

Our single biggest piece of advice to someone coming to speak on the TED stage is to think of their talk not as an opportunity to pitch something (like a business or a cause) but rather as a gift. It is a chance to freely share valuable ideas with the audience. And those ideas have the potential to impact a listener’s life for years to come.

If you possess knowledge that others may benefit from, consider how you could share it to create ripple effects. What may take you a few hours to prepare and act on could light up someone’s life — and that could just be the beginning.

In our connected age, the networks we have access to matter more than ever. Therefore, one of the most important forms of viral generosity is to help people connect with others. The simplest way to do this is to make an introduction.

As psychologist and TED speaker Adam Grant has argued, an introduction can be fairly easy to give — and unbelievably valuable to receive. Ask many people how they met their partner, got their dream job or found the perfect collaborator for their creative project, and the answer will often be the same: someone — a friend, a neighbor, a colleague — introduced them to the right person. What you’re effectively doing is giving someone else access to your network of resources. And those introductions can have exponential consequences.

In his remarkable book Human Universals , anthropologist Donald Brown documented how hospitality is one of hundreds of human behaviors that have been observed in every single culture ever studied. But if hospitality is so ubiquitous (and so pleasant), is it really a form of generosity? Well, yes. Quite apart from any costs involved, it takes effort to invite someone over, whether friends or possible future friends. It’s easier just to watch the next episode of the TV series you’re into.
So how can hospitality contribute to infectious generosity? Hospitality taps into our deepest instincts for connection to one another. And each experience of it evokes a desire to reciprocate.
People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment.

Pioneering artist Lily Yeh was approached by the dancer and choreographer Arthur L. Hall to undertake a community art project in a derelict, abandoned plot in her home city of Philadelphia. “I was interested but totally scared,” Yeh recalled. “I had little resources and no experience in working outdoors in a community setting. I wanted to run away, but I did not want to see a coward in the mirror. So I stepped into the project.”

The community project became the Village of Arts and Humanities, an art park full of trees, sculptures and mosaics created by local adults and children in collaboration with Yeh. Yeh’s work led her to a profound realization: that creating beauty in public spaces is profoundly healing and transformative for communities.

People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment. Those who can enchant can offer a gift of immense value.

好消息：你不必开一堆支票也能成为一个慷慨的人。事实上，许多最令人惊叹、最有效的慷慨典范，都是时间与精力、才华与爱的礼物，是为特定需求量身定制的。这种给予对所有人开放。
许多最令人惊叹、最有效的慷慨典范，都是时间与精力、才华与爱的礼物，是为特定需求量身定制的。
不知从何开始？以下是六种时间与关注的礼物，极有可能引发波及数百万人的涟漪效应，选自TED负责人克里斯·安德森的新书《传染性慷慨》。
1. 转移注意力
禅宗大师一行禅师教导说，注意力是我们能给予他人最珍贵的礼物。慷慨正是从这里开始——愿意停止关注自己，转而关注他人及其需求。从这一联结之举出发，一切皆有可能。
事实是，这并不容易。我们大部分时间都迷失在自己的世界里。我们常常不愿关注他人正在面对的问题。于是我们竖起盾牌。这意味着，许多真正需要我們关注的人，从未感到被我们看见。因此，注意力的慷慨，就是愿意稍微不舒服、放下那些盾牌、付出一些时间、冒险去关心他人的慷慨。
无论你是停下来与需要帮助的人建立有意义的联结，还是花30分钟研究一个你认为可能重要的议题，你都已经踏上了慷慨之旅。
2. 搭建桥梁
在我们这个互联时代，有一种慷慨比以往任何时候都更重要：愿意主动接触与我们意见相左的人。如今许多争端都在网上公开上演。庞大的受众会紧盯网络骂战。如果我们能为更多此类冲突带来令人满意的解决方案，那会怎样？
主动接触批评我们的人很难。这是一种尤其具有挑战性的慷慨心态。你是在牺牲个人的舒适，以求让人们团结在一起的更大善果。但如果你成功了，就会有一个强大的连锁好处：你正在帮助改变当今公共讨论的基调。这是我们所有人的礼物。
我们能给予的唯一最伟大的礼物是知识——解决问题的知识、满足需求的知识，或开辟前路的知

##段落
站上TED演讲台，意味着演讲者不应把演讲视为推销某样东西（比如一项事业或一个企业）的机会，而应把它当作一份礼物。这是一个自由地与观众分享宝贵想法的机会。而这些想法有可能在未来数年里影响听众的人生。

##段落
如果你拥有能让他人受益的知识，想一想你可以如何分享它，从而产生涟漪效应。你花几个小时准备并付诸行动的事情，或许能点亮某个人的人生——而这可能仅仅是个开始。

##段落
4. 促成连接

在这个互联互通的时代，我们所能触及的人脉网络比以往任何时候都更加重要。因此，最具感染力的慷慨行为之一，就是帮助人们与他人建立连接。最简单的方式就是做一次引荐。

##段落
正如心理学家、TED演讲者亚当·格兰特所言，引荐这件事给出时相当容易，收到时却价值无比。问问许多人他们是如何遇见伴侣、获得梦想工作，或为自己的创意项目找到完美合作者的，答案往往如出一辙：某个人——一位朋友、邻居或同事——把他们引荐给了对的人。你实际上做的，是让别人得以进入你的人脉资源网络。而这些引荐可能产生指数级的连锁效应。

##段落
5. 传递好客之道

人类学家唐纳德·布朗在其杰作《人类共通性》中记载，好客之道是被研究过的每一种文化中都观察到的数百种人类行为之一。但既然好客如此普遍（又如此令人愉悦），它真的算一种慷慨吗？答案是肯定的。且不说其中涉及的任何花费，光是邀请别人来做客——无论是朋友还是可能成为朋友的人——就需要付出心力。舒舒服服地追下一集你正在看的剧，显然要轻松得多。

##段落
那么，好客之道如何能促成有感染力的慷慨？好客之道触及了我们内心深处对彼此连接的渴望。而每一次这样的体验，都会唤起一种想要回报的愿望。

##段落
人们固然需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑与超越——这些都是魅力的要素。

##段落
6. 创造魅力

先锋艺术家叶蕾蕾曾受舞蹈家兼编舞家亚瑟·L·霍尔之邀，在她家乡费城一块荒废废弃的地块上开展一个社区艺术项目。“我很感兴趣，但又害怕极了，”叶蕾蕾回忆道，“我资源匮乏，也没有在社区环境中户外工作的经验。我想逃跑，但我不想在镜子里看到一个懦夫。于是我踏入了这个项目。”

##段落
这个社区项目后来成为“艺术与人文村”，一座满是树木、雕塑和马赛克的艺术公园，全部由当地成年人创作。

##段落
她与Yeh合作，为成人和儿童设计项目。Yeh的工作让她深刻意识到：在公共空间创造美，对社区具有深远的疗愈与转化力量。

##段落
人们确实需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑与超越——这些都是“魅力”的要素。能够施展魅力的人，赠予的是一份价值非凡的礼物。

readings.title: Why are more Americans moving to Ireland?
readings.summary: More Americans are now moving to Ireland than Irish people moving to the US
body: 15 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Anne Cassidy In a historic reversal, the number of Americans moving to Ireland last year was higher than the number of Irish people migrating to the US. Was this just a blip or the start of a more profound trend? Michael Sable is an American stand-up comedian and communications manager who moved from Washington DC to Dublin in 2016.  Sable, who draws on his experience of being an American living in the Republic of Ireland in his stand-up routine, says that, when he first arrived, many Irish people he met were surprised he'd made the move, but now they don't question it.  "I've noticed that, as the years go on, people have been less and less incredulous when hearing that an American moved to Ireland," he says.  Sable is one of a rising number of people who have moved to Ireland from the US, with the latest data showing the figure nearly doubling from  4,900 to 9,600 between 2024 and 2025 ,  exceeding the number of Irish people headed in the opposite direction.   It comes as the US saw more people leave than arrive last year, according to a report from US think tank the  Brookings Institution . It said this was the first time that this had been the case "in at least half a century".  The think tank highlighted "dramatic changes in immigration policy" under the second administration of President Trump, including more removals of undocumented foreign workers, and the White House "all but suspend[ing]" the US programme for accepting refugees.    Separately, more American citizens are choosing to move abroad than ever before, says the  Wall Street Journal.  It calculated that "at least 180,000 Americans" voluntarily left the US in 2025, which it said was a record high.   The reversal in the flow of migration between Ireland and the US marks a historic turning point in the shared history of the two countries, which have deep-rooted ties.  For centuries, millions of Irish people emigrated to the US in search of work or a better life, making Irish Americans one of the country's largest ethnic groups. There have been several US presidents with Irish ancestry, including John F Kennedy and Joe Biden, whose visits to Ireland were  celebrated more like homecomings  than diplomatic missions.   Irish writer Colm Tóibín has frequently explored the relationship between Ireland and the US in his work, particularly in his novels, Brooklyn and Long Island, which follow the story of an Irish girl who emigrates to America in the 1950s.  Tóibín, who lives in the US, says the relationship between the US and Ireland has changed. "A myth was created that America was a great place of opportunity and wealth," he says. "It was built into the [Irish] culture that if there's any trouble, you go to England, if there's any ambition or spark you go to America." "The flow of young people [from Ireland to the US] looking for work just hasn't continued. So, that is going to be a big change in the future, because you're not going to get the same easy connection between Ireland and America," he adds.  The trend partly reflects political shifts in both countries. As well as developing into a high-tech, export-driven knowledge economy, Ireland has undergone a social transformation in recent decades, moving from a deeply conservative society to a liberal, progressive nation, following referendums on divorce, abortion and gay marriage.    Tóibín, who was a prominent campaigner for the "yes" vote in Ireland’s same-sex marriage referendum, says: "Everyone became more aware that Ireland was a more liberal, cosmopolitan, open society, and that it would be a good place to live." By contrast, the US has moved to the political right under President Trump, who, since returning to office, has launched a major crackdown on illegal immigration.   Tóibín revisits the Irish-American immigrant experience in his latest short story collection, The News from Dublin. In one story in the collection, Five Bridges, the protagonist is an undocumented Irish immigrant preparing to leave America before US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, known as Ice, come looking for him. The number of Irish citizens deported from the US  rose by more than 50%  in 2025.  "There are large numbers of Irish people in America who are official in every way – they pay taxes, own their own house, have kids in school, but they came in on a tourist visa," says Tóibín. "If Ice found them, Ice would detain them. That's really frightening." Expatsi, a firm that helps US citizens to move abroad,  reported it experienced a month's worth of traffic  in the hours after President Trump's election in 2024. Expatsi co-founder Jen Barnett says the reasons Americans cite for leaving are wide-ranging. "[Factors include] what's going on politically in the US, and has been for 10 years, the cost of living, and then safety. Gun violence is so prevalent," she says.  Politics was also a driving factor for Kevin Wozniak, an American lecturer living in Ireland. He and his husband left Boston in 2023 after he got a post at Maynooth University, 23km (14 miles) west of Dublin.  "My motivation to look at opportunities abroad was deep fears about the trajectory of the country in the era of Donald Trump," Wozniak says. "Ireland has liberalised very significantly and has moved in exactly the opposite direction that the US is moving." Natalia Lange, a migrant support worker based in Crosshaven, county Cork, moved there from Michigan with her husband after the 2024 US election. Lange, who is half-Hungarian and has an EU passport, dreamed of living in Ireland since visiting on a school trip. "Politically, Ireland aligns much more with how we think," she says. "The US has the infrastructure to take in a lot more people, but it's a lot less inviting." Lauren Udoh, from Houston, Texas, moved to Claregalway, in county Galway, in 2021 after marrying her Irish husband. Udoh, who has two young children, works as an executive assistant and documents expat life on social media under the moniker TheGalwayGal.  "One of the biggest benefits is safety. I feel a lot safer here," she says. "With kids going to school, you don’t have to worry about school shootings." Emigration from Ireland has fallen, with 65,600 people leaving in the year to April 2025, a  6% decrease on 2024 , according to the Irish Central Statistics Office (CSO). For those wanting to live abroad, Australia is the most popular destination.  The CSO said 13,500 people left Ireland for Australia in the year to April 2025, the highest level since 2013. This is more than double the estimated 6,100 people who left Ireland for the US, which was, however, still up 22% on the previous year.   Restrictions around J1 visas, which allow Irish university students to work and travel in the US, has caused many  Irish students to rethink studying in the US.    Karen McHugh, CEO at Safe Home Ireland, an organisation supporting Irish-born emigrants wishing to return to Ireland, says: "We've certainly noticed an increase in queries about returning [from the US to Ireland]," she says. "Australia and Canada are two major countries where people are now going to from Ireland, and that's ease of getting a visa." Irish student Jamie McElhinney is currently on a work placement in Portugal as part of his hospitality management course. McElhinney, who studies at Dundalk Institute of Technology, says current immigration controls put him off seeking a work placement in the US. "I was going to go to Boston, and then all of the news about Ice started coming out. It’s a deterrent from going over there," he says.  While there are opportunities in Ireland, with  employment at 74.4%,  there is also a growing housing crisis, with recent  protests  over the shortage of affordable housing.  Barnett says the housing shortage is something the Americans her company helps to relocate are mindful of, adding: "They don't want to add to [the housing crisis], so one of the things we talk to them about is staying out of city centres." Sable, whose Irish grandparents emigrated to the US in 1939, is one of many Americans whose ancestry enabled them to get an Irish passport. Applications for Irish passports in the US rose by 10% in 2024 , the Irish Department of Foreign Affairs reported.  Sable now thinks of Ireland as home. "Culturally, I identify a lot more with Irish people," he says. "It's a very collective society, not huge on individualism like in the US." More like this:  •  Why Ireland's film industry is booming    •  Is New York's cannabis business flying high?   •  The 'brutal' toll of war on Dubai’s tourist trade Bill Hillyard, another American with Irish roots, relocated to Ireland for the cooler climate. He and his wife Anne left California following wildfires in 2019. "My wife said we need to move somewhere where it rains." They now run a pub called The Algiers in Baltimore, Co Cork.  Hillyard says he now tries to avoid turbulent events in the US. "I tried not to follow the news because I'm here now," he says. "But I'm reminded every day, because everyone asks me about Trump and what's going on there… I'm West Cork's ambassador to the US at this point." -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights. ##段落
2026年4月15日 分享 收藏 在Google上设为首选 安妮·卡西迪 去年，移居爱尔兰的美国人数量超过了移居美国的爱尔兰人，这是一次历史性的逆转。这只是一时的反常现象，还是一个更深远趋势的开端？迈克尔·塞布尔是一位美国单口喜剧演员兼传播经理，2016年从华盛顿特区搬到都柏林。塞布尔在脱口秀中融入了自己作为居住在爱尔兰共和国的美国人的经历。他说，初到之时，许多遇到的爱尔兰人都对他做出这一决定感到惊讶，但如今人们已不再质疑。“我注意到，随着时间推移，人们听到美国人移居爱尔兰时，越来越不觉得难以置信了，”他说。塞布尔是从美国移居爱尔兰的人数不断上升的一个缩影。最新数据显示，2024年至2025年间，这一数字从4900人增至9600人，几乎翻了一番，超过了反向移居美国的爱尔兰人数。

##段落
与此同时，根据美国智库布鲁金斯学会的一份报告，去年离开美国的人数多于流入美国的人数。报告称，这是“至少半个世纪以来”首次出现这种情况。该智库强调了特朗普总统第二任期内“移民政策的剧烈变化”，包括加大遣返无证外籍劳工的力度，以及白宫“几乎暂停”了美国接收难民的项目。另据《华尔街日报》报道，越来越多的美国公民选择移居海外。该报测算，2025年“至少有18万美国人”自愿离开美国，称这是历史新高。

##段落
爱尔兰与美国之间移民流向的逆转，标志着两国共同历史中的一个历史性转折点。两国有着深厚的渊源。几个世纪以来，数百万爱尔兰人移居美国寻求工作或更好的生活，使爱尔兰裔美国人成为美国最大的族裔群体之一。多位美国总统拥有爱尔兰血统，包括约翰·F·肯尼迪和乔·拜登，他们对爱尔兰的访问被当作回乡省亲而非外交使命来庆祝。爱尔兰作家科尔姆·托宾在其作品中频繁探讨爱尔兰与美国的关系，尤其是在他的小说《布鲁克林》和《长岛》中，讲述了一位爱尔兰女孩在20世纪50年代移居美国的故事。现居美国的托宾表示，美国与爱尔兰之间的关系已经改变。“人们创造了一个神话，说美国是一个充满机遇和财富的伟大地方，”他说。“这已融入[爱尔兰]文化之中——如果有任何麻烦，你就去英国；如果有任何抱负……”

##段落
“否则你就去美国。”他补充道：“年轻人（从爱尔兰到美国）找工作的潮流并没有延续下去。所以，这将是未来的一个巨大变化，因为爱尔兰和美国之间那种轻松的联系将不复存在。”

##段落
这一趋势部分反映了两国政治的变化。爱尔兰不仅发展成为一个高科技、出口导向的知识经济，近几十年来还经历了社会转型，从一個极度保守的社会转变为一个自由、进步的国家，此前已就离婚、堕胎和同性婚姻举行了全民公投。

##段落
托宾曾是爱尔兰同性婚姻公投中“赞成”票的著名活动家，他说：“每个人都越来越意识到，爱尔兰是一个更自由、更国际化、更开放的社会，是一个宜居的好地方。”相比之下，美国在特朗普总统的领导下转向政治右翼，特朗普自重返白宫以来，已对非法移民展开了大规模打击。

##段落
托宾在他的最新短篇小说集《都柏林消息》中重新审视了爱尔兰裔美国移民的经历。在该集的一个故事《五座桥》中，主人公是一名无证爱尔兰移民，正准备在美国移民和海关执法局（简称Ice）来找他之前离开美国。2025年，被美国驱逐出境的爱尔兰公民人数增加了50%以上。

##段落
“美国有大量爱尔兰人在各方面都是合法的——他们纳税、拥有自己的房子、孩子在上学，但他们是持旅游签证入境的，”托宾说。“如果Ice找到他们，Ice就会拘留他们。这真的很可怕。”帮助美国公民移居国外的公司Expatsi报告称，2024年特朗普总统当选后的几个小时内，其网站流量相当于平时一个月的量。Expatsi联合创始人珍·巴内特表示，美国人给出的离开理由多种多样。

##段落
“[因素包括]美国政治上正在发生的事情，而且已经持续了10年，还有生活成本，然后是安全。枪支暴力如此普遍，”她说。政治也是居住在爱尔兰的美国讲师凯文·沃兹尼亚克的驱动因素。2023年，他在都柏林以西23公里（14英里）的梅努斯大学获得职位后，和丈夫离开了波士顿。

##段落
“我寻求海外机会的动机是对唐纳德·特朗普时代国家发展轨迹的深切担忧，”沃兹尼亚克说。“爱尔兰已经非常显著地自由化了，其发展方向与美国完全相反。”娜塔莉亚·兰格是一名移民支持工作者，常驻科克郡克罗斯黑文，在2024年美国大选后与丈夫从密歇根搬到了那里。兰格有一半匈牙利血统，持有欧盟护照，梦想住在爱尔兰，于是……

##段落
她曾在学校组织的旅行中到访过这里。“在政治上，爱尔兰与我们的想法契合得多，”她说。“美国有接纳更多人的基础设施，但远没有那么友好。”来自得克萨斯州休斯敦的劳伦·乌多在与爱尔兰丈夫结婚后，于2021年搬到了戈尔韦郡的克莱尔戈尔韦。乌多有两个年幼的孩子，担任行政助理，并以“TheGalwayGal”的网名在社交媒体上记录外派生活。“最大的好处之一是安全。我在这里感觉安全多了，”她说。“孩子去上学，你不用担心中学枪击案。”根据爱尔兰中央统计局（CSO）的数据，爱尔兰的移出人数有所下降，截至2025年4月的一年内有65600人离开，较2024年减少6%。对于想移居国外的人来说，澳大利亚是最受欢迎的目的地。CSO表示，截至2025年4月的一年内，有13500人离开爱尔兰前往澳大利亚，为2013年以来的最高水平。这一数字是估计前往美国的6100人的两倍多，不过后者仍比上年增长22%。J1签证（允许爱尔兰大学生在美国工作和旅行）的限制，已促使许多爱尔兰学生重新考虑赴美学习。Safe Home Ireland是一家为希望返回爱尔兰的爱尔兰裔移民提供支持的组织，其首席执行官凯伦·麦休说：“我们确实注意到，关于（从美国返回爱尔兰）的咨询有所增加，”她说。“澳大利亚和加拿大是爱尔兰人现在前往的两个主要国家，因为签证容易获得。”爱尔兰学生杰米·麦克尔希尼目前正在葡萄牙进行工作实习，这是他酒店管理课程的一部分。就读于邓多克理工学院的麦克尔希尼表示，当前的移民管制让他不愿去美国实习。“我本来打算去波士顿，后来关于移民及海关执法局（ICE）的新闻开始不断出现。这让人不敢去那边，”他说。虽然爱尔兰有机会，就业率为74.4%，但也存在日益加剧的住房危机，近期还因经济适用房短缺而爆发抗议。巴尼特说，住房短缺是她公司协助搬迁的美国人会留意的问题，并补充道：“他们不想加剧（住房危机），所以我们与他们谈论的一件事就是不要住在市中心。”萨布尔的祖父母于1939年从爱尔兰移民到美国，她是众多因血统而获得爱尔兰护照的美国人之一。爱尔兰外交部报告称，2024年美国对爱尔兰护照的申请量增长了10%。萨布尔现在把爱尔兰视为家。“在文化上，我认同爱尔兰人多得多，”他说。“这是一个非常……

## 集体社会，不像美国那样极度崇尚个人主义。” 更多类似内容： • 爱尔兰电影产业为何蓬勃发展 • 纽约的大麻生意是否蒸蒸日上？ • 战争对迪拜旅游业的“残酷”冲击 另一位有爱尔兰血统的美国人比尔·希利亚德为了更凉爽的气候搬到了爱尔兰。2019年山火之后，他和妻子安妮离开了加利福尼亚。“我妻子说我们需要搬到一个下雨的地方。”他们现在在科克郡巴尔的摩经营一家名为“阿尔及尔”的酒吧。希利亚德说，他现在尽量避开美国发生的动荡事件。“我尽量不看新闻，因为我现在在这里，”他说。“但我每天都会被提醒，因为每个人都会问我特朗普的事以及那边的情况……我现在都成了西科克驻美国大使了。” -- 欲获取面向董事会及更广泛领域的全球洞察与专家分析，请订阅《商业世界》新闻简报，《精选清单》则为您奉上精心挑选的特稿与洞察。欲了解更多商业及更多内容，请在领英上关注我们。 商业 移民 特稿 商业世界

readings.title: Did the midterms kill MAGA?
readings.summary: Vice President JD Vance gestures as he takes the stage at a campaign rally in Swanton, Ohio, on November 2, 2026. | Tom Brenner/Getty Images
body: Podcasts Did the midterms kill MAGA? A former MAGA acolyte sorts through the wreckage. by Hady Mawajdeh and Noel King Nov 8, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC Gift Vice President JD Vance gestures as he takes the stage at a campaign rally in Swanton, Ohio, on November 2, 2026. Tom Brenner/Getty Images In 2015, Donald Trump descended a golden escalator and launched a presidential campaign that reshaped American politics. More than a decade later, with his record-low approval ratings and the US embroiled in a war with Iran, he asked voters to treat the 2026 midterms as a referendum on him. “Please pretend I’m on the ballot. Because in a way, I am on the ballot,” Trump told a crowd in North Carolina last month. As it turns out, voters did as Trump asked: Democrats won in a landslide, taking control of both chambers of Congress with victories in Republican strongholds like South Carolina and Kansas . Now, Republicans have to decide what those losses mean for the future of the movement Trump built. As Vox’s Andrew Prokop reported , there are already competing explanations for the losses that are taking shape on the right. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vice President JD Vance posted on social media . The conservative commentator Erick Erickson offered a longer list of reasons for the GOP’s failure : “It was also the corruption. The incompetence. The tariffs. The playing nice with Russia. The impression of cruelty. The overly aggressive deportations.” Others emphasized affordability. “Life is too expensive,” right-wing commentator Benny Johnson wrote . “Especially for young people.” Whoever defines what went wrong will likely help determine which parts of Trump’s politics survive, and who gets to lead the presidential ticket in 2028. The conservative writer Rod Dreher has a stake in that debate. He supported Trump in 2024. He’s friends with Vance, and he shares the vice president’s interest in combining social conservatism with economic policies that support families. His critiques come from someone who wanted this administration to succeed. Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Dreher about whether the midterms mean the end of MAGA, what might replace it, and whether Republicans can move past a president who still has two years left in office. Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .

Before the midterm results even came in, you wrote that Republicans were likely to be shellacked and that they had nobody to blame but Donald Trump and themselves. What do you think it is your fellow conservatives need to admit today? That MAGA is over. It’s done. It’s been a failure. It brought Trump to power twice. I think there were some good ideas in MAGA and certainly the old Republican establishment, the pre-Trump establishment, needed to go. But MAGA couldn’t deliver on good government. And if you can’t deliver on good government, it doesn’t matter how charismatic the leader is. It’s not going to work. And I think that there can be no doubt after this week’s election that it was a complete referendum on Donald Trump and he failed. And we have to build from there. You supported Trump in 2024. At the time you wrote that you were aware of some of his failings. I think many people who voted for Trump were aware of some of his failings, but he had a mandate. He had the popular vote, he had the House, he had the Senate. Why couldn’t MAGA, his movement, deliver on good government? “But MAGA couldn’t deliver on good government. And if you can’t deliver on good government, it doesn’t matter how charismatic the leader is.” I think that it all comes down to the fact that Trump made decisions based not on rational calculation, by listening to expert advice, but on gut instinct. I think that the wheels began to fall off of the Trump train on April 2, 2025. That was the so-called Liberation Day when Trump announced these wide tariffs. They weren’t thought out at all. They just came out of his gut. And that set a pattern for the way that Trump made decisions. Plus. he promoted people not based on competence, but based on loyalty to him, personal loyalty. I think this administration has gone from one crisis to another because of that, because Trump doesn’t have a theory or practice of governance. When he came into office, he signed a bunch of executive orders. Some of them did things that I thought were really good, but he didn’t turn them into legislation. This is a guy whose party held both houses of Congress and the White House, yet he just sailed right along as if he was going to be president forever. And then of course, this gets us to the Iran war, which was another gut instinct thing by Trump, which became the symbol for all of the disasters of Trumpism. Can MAGA be divorced from Donald Trump? Can it exist without Donald Trump? No, MAGA is Donald Trump. Donald Trump himself said so. The challenge is going to be, how does the Republican Party rebuild and regroup for 2028 with Trump still in the White House? I mean, think about it. They’re fighting a two-front battle now. You’re going to have to fight the Democrats, who are energized, who are going to come in and make the next two years — justifiably, I would say — about investigating Trump administration corruption. But they’re also going to have to fight Donald Trump himself. Sitting in the White House, he’s not going to shut up. He’s not going to do what is best for his party. He’s going to try to salvage his legacy. What the midterms mean for 2028 What is the next conservative movement? Where do conservatives go from here? The next few months are going to be really interesting in this respect. Until now, everybody on the right has thought that JD Vance, the vice president, is Trump’s natural successor, even though he hasn’t announced whether or not he’s going to run. I think that has now been called severely into question. I say this as someone who’s a personal friend of the vice president and would like to see him be president one day. Nevertheless, even though he strongly opposed the Iran war from behind the scenes, he and Marco Rubio and everyone else in this administration are tied to it and all the other failures of Trumpism. So who does that leave on the outside? I was very surprised, in the past 24 hours, to see and hear Gov. Ron DeSantis, the outgoing governor of Florida, who as we all remember, ran against Trump for the Republican nomination and never stood a chance. He’s not charismatic. He’s super competent, but not charismatic. And so Trump won the 2024 nomination. Well, now DeSantis is coming out making strong, clear, rational critiques of MAGA and Trumpism. And I think that DeSantis could be the outside candidate who has the best [chance] because he’s the only national Republican politician not tainted by Trumpism. JD Vance is a friend of yours. He’s credited you with getting him involved in politics. You say you’d like to see him be president. I think a legitimate question following what we’ve seen over the past two years and then last night is why? Why do you want JD Vance to be president? JD Vance has been associated with the national conservatism movement, as have I — the movement started by Yoram Hazony, which has been about prioritizing national sovereignty, national interest, a cultural conservatism that is also in favor of economic reforms to make it easier to raise families. JD Vance has been the avatar for that sort of conservatism. I see the bones of this kind of conservatism within Trump and MAGA, but it got completely crushed by Trump’s own obsessions. If JD can go back to the man I think he is deep down and start to champion this sort of thing — more of a pro-family economic liberalism with social conservatism and no new wars — if it’s possible for any Republican to claim that now, then I think that he could have a chance. I think he is a good man. I have criticized him publicly, in print, as a friend for not separating himself from the bigots on the dissident right — the antisemites and the white nationalists. This extremist crowd is going to make a bid for power in the rubble of MAGA. And I think whether it’s JD or whoever becomes a Republican standard bearer is going to have to face them down. We’ve talked about JD Vance. We have talked about Ron DeSantis. They represent different things within conservatism. Tucker Carlson represents something else within conservatism. I think it’s something you don’t like very much. And, um, and then there’s Marco Rubio, who represents something that we were all familiar with from the early aughts. What do you think of these two other boldface names as we head into 2028? Tucker Carlson has beclowned himself, and it’s really sad. As someone who used to be friends with him, I thought he was a sensible, interesting commentator who often said a lot of common-sense things. But sometime in the last couple of years, he lost his mind and became antisemitic and just a crazy conspiracy theorist. A lot of people are worried about his influence on the vice president because they’ve been close for years. Tucker was key in getting Donald Trump to choose JD Vance as vice president. I have no inside knowledge of that at all, but it worries me as well. I think JD is his own man, but it’s going to be very hard for JD going forward to maintain viability as a potential Republican Party leader until and unless he addresses the Tucker Carlson problem. I don’t think Tucker’s going to run for president. If he did that, he could only be a spoiler, and I don’t think he actually wants it. In Marco Rubio’s case, he’s been a real chameleon. He was against MAGA. He was the neocon’s neocon for a while, but he has been a faithful servant and executor of Trump’s foreign policy. And for some reason, it doesn’t seem to have stuck to him the way it has stuck to JD Vance. I’m not sure why that is, but with all of these guys who have been part of the Trump administration, it’s gonna be very, very hard to cut that albatross from around their neck. One of the dynamics that we’ve seen in the Trump era over the last decade is that Republicans in Congress don’t want to stand up to Donald Trump. They don’t want to cross him. What should Republicans in Congress do? Should they finally grow a spine and say, “ Look, we don’t have to obey every single thing that President Trump says ”? Absolutely. I mean, what do they have to lose now? Trump has never been loyal to anybody who’s pledged loyalty to him. Greg Abbott, the three-term governor of Texas who lost his bid for reelection — no sooner had the election been called and Trump put out a statement calling him a RINO . Trump is not loyal. And so there is nothing in it left for Republicans to stick with him. He’s not going to be a factor in 2028. Maybe they want his endorsement in the 2028 primaries. Really? After this? That would be the kiss of death. Republicans are now, and Congress is now, going to have to find a spine and stand up and establish some independence. If they had done that earlier, we might not be in the situation today.
