readings.title: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
readings.summary: Being incredibly talented doesn’t immunize you against anxiety, but Lionel Messi has mastered a coping mechanism that's also a tactical weap
body: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
What separates the very best in the world from the remaining 7 billion of us?

Exceptional talent often looks like an act of revolution — a person doing something in a way no one has ever done it before — but many revolutionary talents are actually built on a foundation of evolutionary tweaks. These tweaks develop over time, often compensating for weaknesses and anxieties that might derail a lesser talent.
For all his brilliance, though, Messi is famously anxious. For several years, he habitually vomited on the field before big matches.

Take the world’s best soccer player, an Argentinean named Lionel Messi. Messi has won more Ballon d’Or trophies, awarded to the best soccer player of the year, than any other player. He has scored more goals in a calendar year than any other living player, is the top all-time scorer in Spain’s La Liga, and has the highest goal ratio in the sport today, scoring almost once every match.

For all his brilliance, though, he’s famously anxious. For several years, Messi habitually vomited on the field before big matches. After a string of disappointing national-team losses, another former Argentinean giant of the game, the late Diego Maradona, uncharitably criticized Messi by suggesting that it was “useless trying to make a leader out of a man who goes to the toilet twenty times before a game.”

Being incredibly talented doesn’t immunize you against anxiety, and many of the world’s best grapple with anxiety precisely because they expect so much from themselves. But Messi hasn’t allowed his anxiety to diminish his brilliance because he’s mastered a coping mechanism that also doubles as the secret behind his tactical brilliance.
Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Second, he scopes out the opposition.

A soccer match runs for 90 minutes (plus a few minutes for “injury time”), and most players are active in the game from the first minute. As soon as the whistle blows, they implore their teammates to pass the ball and pursue the tactics their coaches laid out before the game.

But Messi is famous for not playing the game during its opening minutes. This is his evolutionary tweak, which developed as he played the game at progressively higher levels. For the opening minutes, Messi ambles back and forth near the middle of the field and almost never engages with his teammates. Whereas other players run and sometimes sprint, Messi spends much of his time walking, rarely breaking into more than a slow jog.

Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Easing into the game is Messi’s way of ensuring he’s fully engaged for the remainder of the game. His on-field vomiting has resolved itself, in part perhaps because he’s found a more effective way to calm his nerves. Second, he spends this time scoping out the opposition. His legs move slowly, but his eyes dart from player to player, assessing his opponents’ strengths, weaknesses, and tactics, and monitoring his own team’s movement with and around the ball. Messi is less valuable to his team early in the game, but this tactical pause elevates his value for the remaining 95 percent of the game.

If you split soccer game play into “preparatory” and “engaged” components, Messi leans heavily on preparation. During one classic game between Messi’s Barcelona and archrivals Real Madrid, in 2017, Messi ran for just four minutes and walked for more than eighty of the game’s ninety minutes. When he was engaged, though, he was dynamic, creating nine chances, scoring one goal, and feeding the ball to a teammate who scored another goal.
As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act.

That pattern isn’t unusual for Messi, and it’s often in the biggest games that he accentuates his in-game preparation. That preparation also explains his ability to find himself in the right place at the right time, over and over. Though his positional play appears otherworldly, it isn’t a miracle; it’s that he’s learned, minute by minute, that a particular defender leaves a particular square of pitch uncovered or that two midfielders leave a small corner of the pitch open when they gravitate to the middle of the field.
The lesson for the rest of us is clear: When you’re anxious, whether in athletics or in life more broadly, pause. Slow down . Prepare.

As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act. Judson Brewer, a psychiatrist and neuroscientist, has spent much of his career thinking about how to do nothing.
About fifteen years ago, Brewer developed a mindfulness-based treatment for addiction.
His approach instructs addicts to resist the waves of anxiety during moments of craving by following the four steps of an approach that goes by the acronym RAIN:
I nvestigate your emotions and thoughts (e.g., “What is happening in my body now?”)
N ote what is happening from moment to moment.

Brewer has said that his approach was inspired by clinical psychologist Tara Brach’s . To test the approach, Brewer worked with smokers who were struggling to quit. Nicotine addiction is notoriously stubborn — more so than many harder drugs that produce stronger immediate responses in users.

Before unleashing the program on smokers, Brewer wanted to test the system on himself. The problem was “I was a nonsmoker,” Brewer wrote, “who needed to be able to relate to patients who felt as though their heads were going to explode unless they smoked.”

Nicotine has a half-life of around two hours, so to begin, smokers need to resist the urge to light up for two hours at a time. Brewer reasoned that smokers who could last two hours without a cigarette would cultivate new nonsmoking habits, extending those stretches till they no longer felt the urge to smoke at all.

He simulated these periods of resistance by learning to meditate for two-hour stretches without moving. During moments of restlessness, he followed the RAIN steps — recognize, allow, investigate, note — and if he moved his body, the clock would reset, and he’d have to start again.

This might sound easy, but two hours is a long time to sit still without entertainment. “Surprisingly it wasn’t the physical pain of not shifting for a long time that got me,” Brewer wrote. “It was the restlessness … Those cravings shouted, ‘Get up!’ ”
Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean.

For many months, Brewer would get close, then restlessness would defeat him. “Then one day,” he wrote, “I did it. I sat for the full two hours … Each subsequent sit got easier and easier because I had the confidence that it could be done. And I knew that my patients could quit smoking. They simply needed the proper tools.”

Brewer was right. His patients had been stuck, incapable of quitting one of the most addictive substances on earth. But when he ran study after study, pitting his RAIN mindfulness method against the most effective addiction treatment approaches of the day, his approach was more than twice as effective.

Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean. They were more than five times as likely to have shaken their addictions using an approach that essentially taught them to pause at the moment their bodies were most urgently driving them to act.

Of the four steps in Brewer’s RAIN approach, the second — allowing — is perhaps the most critical. Allowing an experience to wash over you sounds disarmingly easy because it doesn’t require you to do anything. But that’s exactly the point. It’s difficult because you’re forced to do nothing despite the urge to act.

以世界上最优秀的足球运动员、阿根廷人莱昂内尔·梅西为例。梅西获得的颁发给年度最佳足球运动员的金球奖杯数量超过任何其他球员。他在一个自然年内的进球数超过任何其他在世球员，是西班牙甲级联赛的历史最佳射手，并且拥有当今足坛最高的进球率——几乎每场比赛进一球。
然而，尽管才华横溢，他却以焦虑著称。有几年时间，梅西习惯性地在大赛前于球场上呕吐。在一连串令人失望的国家队失利之后，另一位阿根廷足球传奇、已故的迭戈·马拉多纳毫不留情地批评梅西，暗示“试图把一个赛前要上二十次厕所的人培养成领袖是徒劳的”。
天赋异禀并不能让你对焦虑免疫，世界上许多最优秀的人恰恰因为对自己期望太高而与焦虑搏斗。但梅西没有让焦虑削弱他的光芒，因为他掌握了一种应对机制，而这同时也是他战术天才背后的秘密。
在这些开场几分钟里，梅西做了两件事。第一，他让自己平静下来。第二，他观察对手。
一场足球比赛持续90分钟（加上几分钟“伤停补时”），大多数球员从第一分钟起就积极参与比赛。哨声一响，他们就催促队友传球，执行教练赛前布置的战术。
但梅西以在开场几分钟不参与比赛而闻名。这就是他的渐进式微调，随着他在越来越高的水平上踢球而逐渐形成。在开场几分钟里，梅西在球场中部附近来回踱步，几乎从不与队友配合。其他球员奔跑、有时冲刺，而梅西大部分时间都在走路，很少加速到超过慢跑的节奏。

##段落
这是ssi确保自己在比赛剩余时间里完全投入的方式。他在场上呕吐的情况已经自行缓解，部分原因也许是他找到了更有效的办法来平复紧张情绪。其次，他利用这段时间摸清对手的底细。他的双腿缓慢移动，但目光却在球员之间来回扫视，评估对手的强弱与战术，同时观察本方队友的跑位以及围绕球的移动。比赛初期，梅西对球队的价值较低，但这段战术性的停顿提升了他在剩余95%比赛时间里的价值。

##段落
如果把足球比赛拆分为“准备”和“投入”两个部分，梅西严重倚重准备。2017年梅西所在的巴塞罗那与死敌皇家马德里的一场经典比赛中，梅西只跑了四分钟，而在九十分钟的比赛里走了八十多分钟。然而当他投入时，他极具爆发力，创造了九次机会，攻入一球，并助攻队友再进一球。

##段落
可以想见，停顿比听起来要难。面对沉默与焦虑，我们的本能是行动。

##段落
这种模式对梅西来说并不罕见，而且往往是在最重大的比赛中，他更会强化自己的场上准备。这种准备也解释了为何他能一次又一次地出现在正确的位置上。尽管他的位置感看似超凡脱俗，但这并非奇迹；而是他逐分钟地摸清了某位后卫会漏掉哪块草皮，或者两名中场球员在向球场中路靠拢时会留出哪一小块空当。

##段落
给我们其他人的启示很清楚：当你焦虑时，无论是在运动中还是在更广泛的生活中，都要停顿。放慢节奏。做好准备。

##段落
可以想见，停顿比听起来要难。面对沉默与焦虑，我们的本能是行动。精神病学家兼神经科学家贾德森·布鲁尔职业生涯的大部分时间都在思考如何做到“什么都不做”。

##段落
大约十五年前，布鲁尔开发了一种基于正念的成瘾治疗方法。

##段落
他的方法指导成瘾者在渴求发作时，通过遵循一个缩写为RAIN的四步法来抵御焦虑的浪潮：

##段落
Recognize what is arising.（识别正在升起的是什么。）

##段落
Allow it to be there.（允许它存在。）

##段落
Investigate your emotions and thoughts (e.g., "What is happening in my body now?")（探究你的情绪和想法，例如“我身体里现在发生了什么？”）

##段落
Note what is happening from moment to moment.（留意每时每刻正在发生什么。）

##段落
布鲁尔曾说，他的方法受到临床心理学家塔拉·布拉赫的启发。为了检验这一方法，布鲁尔与正在努力戒烟的吸烟者合作。尼古丁成瘾出了名地顽固——比许多在使用者体内产生更强即时反应的硬性毒品还要顽固。

##段落
在全面推行该项目之前

##段落
布鲁尔想在自己身上测试这套方法，对象是吸烟者。问题在于，“我是一个不吸烟的人，”布鲁尔写道，“却需要能够理解那些觉得除非抽烟否则脑袋就要炸开的患者。”

##段落
尼古丁的半衰期约为两小时，因此一开始，吸烟者需要一次抵制两小时想点烟的冲动。布鲁尔推断，能坚持两小时不抽烟的吸烟者会培养出新的不吸烟习惯，逐渐延长这些时间段，直到完全不再有吸烟的冲动。

##段落
他通过练习冥想、连续两小时不动来模拟这些抵制期。在躁动不安的时刻，他遵循RAIN步骤——识别、允许、探究、标注——如果他动了身体，计时就会重置，他必须重新开始。

##段落
这听起来可能很容易，但两个小时一动不动、没有任何娱乐，是一段很长的时间。“出乎意料的是，让我难受的并不是长时间不挪动的身体疼痛，”布鲁尔写道，“而是躁动不安……那些渴望在喊：‘起来！’”

##段落
几个月后，当其他治疗方案上的大多数患者已经复吸时，他的正念小组依然保持戒断。

##段落
有好几个月，布鲁尔总是接近成功，然后躁动不安打败了他。“然后有一天，”他写道，“我做到了。我坐满了整整两个小时……之后每一次静坐都越来越容易，因为我有信心这件事是可以做到的。而且我知道我的患者能够戒烟。他们只是需要合适的工具。”

##段落
布鲁尔是对的。他的患者一直困在原地，无法戒掉地球上最容易上瘾的物质之一。但当他开展一项又一项研究，将自己的RAIN正念方法与当时最有效的成瘾治疗方法进行对比时，他的方法效果高出一倍多。

##段落
几个月后，当其他治疗方案上的大多数患者已经复吸时，他的正念小组依然保持戒断。他们戒除成瘾的可能性高出五倍多，而这种方法本质上就是教他们在身体最迫切驱使他们行动的那一刻暂停下来。

##段落
在布鲁尔RAIN方法的四个步骤中，第二步——允许——或许是最关键的。让一种体验冲刷而过，听起来容易得令人放松警惕，因为它不要求你做任何事情。但这恰恰是关键所在。它之所以困难，是因为你被迫在有力行动冲动的情况下什么都不做。

##段落
然而，尽管暂停和准备有诸多好处，有时主要事件并不会按计划进行。梅西输掉了无数场比赛，而布鲁尔的尼古丁成瘾者在他的实验结束数周或数月后也并非全都保持戒断。掌握这些失败之后的焦虑和不适至关重要，而这也是最

body: America, Actually How Democrats can make good on their new mandate Maryland Gov. Wes Moore explains what his party needs to do in the wake of their midterm victories. by Jacob Brogan and Astead Herndon Nov 7, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Gift Maryland Gov. Wes Moore is often mentioned as a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2028, speculation that he has not exactly batted down. Monica Morgan/Getty Images The midterm elections were great for Democrats everywhere, but some triumphed even more decisively than others: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, for example, cruised to reelection with roughly 63 percent of the vote. Voters pushed Republicans out — and kept Democrats like Moore in power — in part because of their concerns over a handful of critical issues, including the rising cost of living, the Iran war, and the growing dominance of AI and data centers. The question now is how Democrats can best wield their new power to act on the currents that carried them into office. For Moore, the stakes may be particularly high: He’s often mentioned as a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2028, speculation that he has not exactly batted down . America, Actually host Astead Herndon spoke with Moore about his vision for how the Democrats should proceed. As Moore put it, this is a moment in which the party will have to move quickly on the problems that motivate voters most. Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel . Lowering cost is the top priority for voters, and, frankly, it was where they penalized Trump the most. What’s the single biggest thing Democrats could do to address folks’ cost of living concerns? Actually move fast to fix the things. No more studies. No more 10-year research reports. Move fast. For example, in Maryland, we’ve done permitting reform to be able to speed up affordable housing, right? And I did not need a 10-year research paper to tell me that we have an issue with affordable housing. Get more housing around transit. Do more transit-oriented development. If it’s state-owned land, don’t tell me why we can’t do something. It is state owned land. Do something on it. The reason we made the largest investments in childcare in our state’s history is because it is insane when you’re watching the fact that people are spending thirty and forty percent of their paychecks on child care and knowing how much that’s actually going to impact [them]. So there are things that we can do right now to be able to address it. But I also think that there are things that we need Washington to be able to do. For example, gas prices: There’s no governor that can impact gas prices. We just need to stop fighting stupid wars. There’s no governor that is impacting national energy policy or national grocery prices. What we need to do is stop allowing illegal tariff policy to happen. So I do think that there are things that Washington Democrats have got to do, and that they need to move fast on. But I also think that we don’t need to wait for them to be able to put things in place that we know that actually work. I wonder what universal healthcare means to you. Is that the government providing insurance? If you look at what we’ve done here in Maryland, we’ve been able to actually come up with platforms through our Total Cost of Care [Model]. We’re actually working with our hospitals. Our hospitals have a universal budget, and are then able to make sure that people are getting the care that they need. That has done a tremendous job of being able to help to break the cost curve. Maryland is one of the only states in the country where you’re watching the cost of healthcare actually go down, [while] also being able to increase coverage. A lot of the Democrats’ affordability message came out of Mamdani’s win. I remember him telling me the one thing he would never budge on is the belief that billionaires shouldn’t exist. I wanted to pose that question to you. Do you think billionaires should exist? I lose no sleep over the amount of billionaires in our society. I do lose sleep over the amount of children that are growing up in poverty. And I think those who [do] have, have a responsibility to support and uplift and create pathways for those who do not. Here in our state, we actually cut taxes for the middle class. We cut taxes for military veterans. And I said [to wealthy Marylanders], you need to invest more to make sure that we’re doing things like we’re doing: having the fastest public safety turnaround story in the United States of America, having math and reading scores in our public schools now at five-year highs. And I did ask wealthy Marylanders to invest a little bit more to make sure we can get those kinds of results. What Democrats could actually do to lower your healthcare costs I wanted to move on to Iran. You served in Afghanistan and are a veteran. When we think about this incoming Democratic Congress, should they continue funding a war that Americans have mostly found is not in their interest? No, and they shouldn’t have funded in the first place. I’ve heard the argument that that leaves soldiers behind. No, because we’re talking about a president who unilaterally went to war without even asking Congress for authority. The president does not have the authority to just wage war by himself. That is something that the Constitution lays out. Congress is the only one that has the authority for that. And truthfully, this Congress has been so caught up in the aura of the president of the United States that they have not been leaders; they have been cheerleaders. Part of the issue is that this Congress needs to be held to account, and that’s exactly what I think happened on Tuesday. But I think about my experiences, right? I served in Afghanistan. I led soldiers with the 82nd Airborne Division, and we went over there with what we believed was an understanding of what was at stake and what needed to happen. That this was about the Taliban, and the Taliban could not be in charge of Afghanistan after 9/11. Twenty years later, trillions of dollars spent, thousands of American service members dead, and do you know who’s in charge of Afghanistan right now? The Taliban. And so we are dragging ourselves again into another forever war. And the problem is that we have a Congress that is not actually asserting its authority to be able to check this administration. I think that Congress needs to get this done not in the first hundred days, [but] in the first hundred hours. Congress needs to assert its authority and say to the president of the United States: This needs to end. Data centers also had a horrible night on Tuesday. But I still hear a lot of Democrats say that AI has a place in the economy of tomorrow. Is there a place for pro-AI Democrats in this big tent? I am very concerned about what we’ve seen from AI, and I know a lot of Americans are. I’m hopeful for what I think the promise of what AI can bring to things like health care and what I think AI can bring to things like education. But I also know that there need to be guardrails. What we have seen from Donald Trump and these folks is that there are no guardrails. They just let it do what it does. I don’t think that’s the right answer. I think that’s remarkably dangerous. I don’t think that the answer is telling them, “Police yourself, guys, because that’s going to get us to the right answer.” And that’s why in Maryland, we’ve actually put together guidelines as to how we’re going to be protected from AI. That includes things like protecting our workforce. That includes things like protecting our pocketbooks. That includes things like protecting our children. We put together some of the most stringent guidelines in the country that said things like, they have to pay for all their own energy and all their own upgrades. That our taxpayers do not pay a single penny for that. That they cannot pollute our air or pollute our water. They need to follow all environmental guidelines. That they need to hire local union workers. And also really importantly, that we need to make sure that the people of Maryland have control, not the data center companies, not the Trump administration. That control belongs to us. About half of the local jurisdictions in Maryland have either a ban or a pause on [data centers]. And I’ve said the state will never override you, ever. If you have a ban or a pause, that is done, because control goes to the locals. ##段落
美国，实际上 民主党人如何才能兑现他们的新授权 马里兰州州长韦斯·摩尔解释了他的政党在中期选举获胜后需要做什么。作者：雅各布·布罗根和阿斯特德·赫恩登 2026年11月7日，下午1:00 UTC 赠礼 马里兰州州长韦斯·摩尔经常被提及为2028年民主党总统候选人的潜在人选，而他本人也并未完全否认这一猜测。莫妮卡·摩根/盖蒂图片社

##段落
中期选举对各地的民主党人来说都是大好事，但有些人的胜利更为决定性：例如，马里兰州州长韦斯·摩尔以约63%的得票率轻松赢得连任。选民把共和党人赶下台——并让像摩尔这样的民主党人继续掌权——部分原因是他们对几个关键问题的担忧，包括不断上涨的生活成本、伊朗战争，以及人工智能和数据中心日益增强的主导地位。现在的问题是，民主党人如何才能最好地运用他们的新权力，顺应那些将他们推上执政位置的潮流。对摩尔来说，赌注可能尤其高：他经常被提及为2028年民主党总统候选人的潜在人选，而他本人也并未完全否认这一猜测。《美国，实际上》主持人阿斯特德·赫恩登与摩尔谈论了他对民主党应如何推进的愿景。正如摩尔所说，这是一个政党必须迅速应对最激励选民的问题的时刻。以下是他们对话的节选，为长度和清晰度做了编辑。完整节目还有更多内容，所以请在您获取播客的任何平台收听《美国，实际上》，或在Vox的YouTube频道观看。

##段落
降低生活成本是选民的首要任务，而且坦率地说，这也是他们最严厉惩罚特朗普的地方。民主党人能做的最重要的一件事是什么，以解决人们对生活成本的担忧？

##段落
实际上要迅速行动，解决问题。不要再研究了。不要再搞十年期的研究报告了。迅速行动。例如，在马里兰州，我们做了许可改革，以加快经济适用房的建设，对吧？我不需要一份十年期的研究论文来告诉我，我们在经济适用房方面有问题。在公共交通周边建更多住房。做更多以公共交通为导向的开发。如果是州有土地，不要告诉我为什么我们不能做某事。这是州有土地。在上面做点什么。我们在州历史上对儿童保育做出最大投资的原因，是因为当你看到人们把工资的百分之三十到四十花在儿童保育上，并且知道这实际上会对他们产生多大影响时，这简直疯了。所以我们现在就可以做一些事情来应对这个问题。但我也认为，有些事我们需要华盛顿来做。例如，汽油价格：没有哪个州长能影响汽油价格。我们只是需要

##段落
停止打愚蠢的战争。没有哪个州长能影响国家能源政策或全国食品价格。我们需要做的是不再让非法的关税政策发生。所以我确实认为，华盛顿的民主党人有必须做的事情，而且需要快速推进。但我也认为，我们不必等待他们才能把我们知道确实有效的措施落实到位。我想知道全民医疗对你意味着什么。是政府提供保险吗？如果你看看我们在马里兰州所做的工作，我们实际上通过我们的总护理成本模型想出了各种平台。我们实际上正在与我们的医院合作。我们的医院有统一预算，因此能够确保人们获得他们所需的护理。这在帮助打破成本曲线方面做得非常出色。马里兰州是全国仅有的几个你看到医疗成本实际下降、同时还能扩大覆盖面的州之一。民主党的许多可负担性信息都源自马姆达尼的胜利。我记得他告诉我，他永远不会让步的一件事就是认为亿万富翁不应该存在。我想把这个问题提给你。你认为亿万富翁应该存在吗？我不会因为我们社会中的亿万富翁数量而失眠。我确实会因为大量儿童在贫困中长大而失眠。而且我认为那些拥有财富的人有责任支持、提升并为那些没有的人创造路径。在我们州，我们实际上为中产阶级减税。我们为退伍军人减税。我对富有的马里兰人说，你们需要更多投资，以确保我们正在做的事情，比如：拥有全美最快的公共安全改善故事，让我们公立学校的数学和阅读成绩现在达到五年来的最高水平。我确实要求富有的马里兰人多投资一点，以确保我们能取得这样的结果。民主党人实际上可以做什么来降低你的医疗成本。我想转到伊朗问题。你曾在阿富汗服役，是一名退伍军人。当我们想到这个即将上任的民主党国会时，他们应该继续资助一场美国人大多认为不符合自身利益的战争吗？不，而且他们一开始就不应该资助。我听到过一种说法，说那会让士兵被抛下。不，因为我们谈论的是一位单方面发动战争、甚至没有向国会请求授权的总统。总统没有权力独自发动战争。这是宪法规定的。国会是唯一拥有这一权力的机构。而且说实话，这届国会一直

readings.title: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
readings.summary: What does leadership look like? While there are various approaches to leading a team, many of us land on common questions in the search for
body: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
" data-large-file="https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770" /> Maria Petrishina / iStock

While there are various approaches to leading a team, many of us land on common questions in the search for an effective leadership style: How can I be there for my team? Do I need to command respect, or earn it? And the most crucial question of all: How can I make sure that my team trusts me?

Cady Coleman has been confronting these questions throughout her career as a chemist, engineer, Air Force colonel and astronaut. In conversation with TED science curator David Biello, Coleman shared three strategies to establish — and maintain — trust in a leader. Whatever your career is, these tips can help you to prepare your team to face any challenge you come across — in outer space or here on Earth.
People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team” … But maybe there should be.
1. Be brave enough to get to know your team members as individuals

People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team”… But maybe there should be, says Coleman. Every member of your team is a whole person, and since so many of the problems we face at work are interdisciplinary, understanding who each individual is beyond the 9-to-5 is valuable. Being vulnerable enough to get to know your team this way is an essential skill for any leader.

When you are able to say, “I think your world is different from mine, and I’d like to understand more about it,” you’re not just building trust; you’re opening a communication channel that teaches you more about your teammate’s qualities, says Coleman. This type of conversation requires the willingness and bravery to be vulnerable. Once you know what everyone brings to the table, you can foster the growth of qualities that can lead the team to collective success.

For example, as Coleman prepared for life on the space station, her advisors warned that the long periods of time away from family might be too much to handle. For her, however, this wasn’t a problem — she had been commuting and working away from her family for more than a decade. After sharing her experience, her colleagues realized she’d not only be adaptable to life on the space station, but also she could help others cope with the change, too.
2. Create a culture that’s open to everyone’s ideas
While leaders have to guide their teams, it’s equally important to let everyone know that they can advocate for themselves and bring their own ideas to the table.

Coleman benefitted from such leadership at NASA when she was training to go to the space station. In the face of budget cuts, NASA announced that they’d be eliminating their smaller space suits, meaning that if someone wasn’t qualified to use a larger space suit, they couldn’t go to the space station. This presented a choice for Coleman: wait for NASA to acquire suits that fit her or figure out how she could train in the larger suits. By working with NASA’s decision makers, Coleman was able to shift her training to use the bigger suits. Had she not felt the freedom to speak up, she says, she would have been waiting 10 years to go to the space station in a small suit.
When you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily.

Sometimes establishing trust in the workplace can be more difficult than you expect, but when you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily. Workplace dynamics are always changing — maybe a teammate’s work/life priorities have shifted, or a big mistake requires you all to work together under new pressures. These challenges make fostering trust tricky, but they are also moments of opportunity.

If a new challenge has arisen or trust has been breached, Coleman reminds us to “always figure out the why and the what.” Make sure to ask: why has this happened, why do they feel this way, and what can be done about it? Be open to different points of view, and don’t give up if you don’t get through at first. Connection is often in the smaller things you do; talk about food or music, write a note to compliment an idea and ask to hear more. This level of connection and vulnerability may not seem intuitive at first, but as you make trust a core part of your mission, it becomes easy.

Trust, Coleman reminds us, is both given and earned. As a woman, she knew gaining the trust of some male colleagues might be extra challenging. Her approach was simple: she performed well and, with patience and persistence, learned her colleagues’ language and taught them hers. The challenges in gaining trust will always be there, but if you model vulnerability, openness and understanding for your team, you’ll find the rewards will always be there, too.

This post was adapted from a recent LinkedIn Live conversation with Cady Coleman, former NASA Astronaut and author of the forthcoming book, Sharing Space: An Astronaut’s Guide to Mission, Wonder, and Making Change , due out July 2024.

成为高效领导者的3个策略，来自一位前宇航员
2023年12月4日

" data-large-file="https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770" /> 玛丽亚·佩特里希娜 / iStock
领导力是什么样子的？
虽然带领团队有各种不同的方式，但我们在寻找有效领导风格时，往往会落到一些共同的问题上：我怎样才能支持我的团队？我需要命令尊重，还是赢得尊重？而最关键的问题是：我怎样才能确保我的团队信任我？
卡迪·科尔曼在她的职业生涯中一直在面对这些问题——作为化学家、工程师、空军上校和宇航员。在与TED科学策展人 David Biello 的对话中，科尔曼分享了三个建立并维持领导者信任的策略。无论你从事什么职业，这些建议都能帮助你让团队做好准备，去面对你们遇到的任何挑战——无论是在外太空还是在地球上。
人们常说，“团队里没有‘我’”……但也许应该有。
1. 勇敢地去了解你的团队成员作为个体
人们常说，“团队里没有‘我’”……但科尔曼说，也许应该有。你团队中的每个成员都是一个完整的人，而且由于我们在工作中面临的许多问题都是跨学科的，了解每个人在朝九晚五之外是谁是很有价值的。愿意以这种方式展现脆弱去了解你的团队，是任何领导者的一项基本技能。
科尔曼说，当你能够说出“我认为你的世界和我的不同，我想更多地了解它”时，你不仅是在建立信任；你还在打开一条沟通渠道，让你更多地了解队友的品质。这类对话需要意愿和勇气去展现脆弱。一旦你了解了每个人能带来什么，你就可以培养那些能带领团队走向集体成功的品质。
例如，当科尔曼为空间站生活做准备时，她的顾问们警告说，长时间远离家人可能难以承受。然而对她来说，这不是问题——她已经通勤并在远离家人的情况下工作了十多年。在分享了自己的经历后，她的同事们意识到，她不仅能适应空间站的生活，还能帮助其他人应对这种变化。
2. 创造一种对所有人想法都开放的文化
虽然领导者必须引导他们的团队，但同样重要的是让每个人知道，他们可以为自己发声，并把自己的想法摆到桌面上。
科尔曼在美国宇航局接受太空训练时，就受益于这样的领导方式

##段落
面对预算削减，NASA宣布将取消较小尺寸的宇航服，这意味着如果有人不具备使用较大宇航服的资格，就无法前往空间站。这给科尔曼带来了一个选择：要么等待NASA采购适合她的宇航服，要么想办法穿着较大的宇航服进行训练。通过与NASA的决策者沟通协作，科尔曼成功将自己的训练调整为使用较大尺寸的宇航服。她说，如果她当时没有畅所欲言的自由，她可能要等上10年才能穿着小号宇航服前往空间站。
##段落
当你把建立信任作为核心目标时，其余的事情就会水到渠成。
##段落
3. 把信任当作你的使命
##段落
有时候，在工作场所建立信任可能比你预想的更困难，但当你把建立信任作为核心目标时，其余的事情就会水到渠成。职场动态始终在变化——也许某位队友的工作/生活重心发生了转移，或者一个重大失误要求大家在新压力下协同合作。这些挑战让培养信任变得棘手，但它们同时也是机遇。
##段落
如果出现了新的挑战，或者信任已被破坏，科尔曼提醒我们“始终要弄清楚原因和内容”。务必问自己：为什么会发生这件事，他们为什么会有这种感受，以及能对此做些什么？对不同观点保持开放心态，如果一开始没有沟通成功，也不要放弃。联结往往体现在你做的小事中；聊聊美食或音乐，写张便条称赞某个想法并请对方多说一些。这种程度的联结和坦诚起初可能并不直观，但当你把信任作为使命的核心部分时，它就会变得容易。
##段落
科尔曼提醒我们，信任既是给予的，也是赢得的。作为一名女性，她知道赢得某些男性同事的信任可能格外具有挑战性。她的方法很简单：她表现出色，并以耐心和坚持学习同事的语言，同时也教他们理解自己的语言。赢得信任的挑战永远存在，但如果你为团队展现坦诚、开放和理解，你会发现回报也永远存在。
